stories.body:
During the 30 years of the Troubles, policing in Northern Ireland was a major area of division. The Good Friday agreement brought big changes in policing and justice, including the creation of the Police Service of Northern Ireland. This replaced the Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC), 25 years ago on November 4 2001.

At the time of the agreement in 1998, only around 8% of the RUC was Catholic – a community which made up roughly 40% of Northern Ireland’s population. While the IRA’s campaign to target and kill police officers undoubtedly deterred Catholic participation, so did the perceived unionist orientation of the organisation itself.

The agreement resulted in the Independent Commission on Policing, chaired by Conservative politician Chris Patten. This recommended a “new start” – a police service which would be representative and have the confidence of both communities.

Following radical structural and symbolic change, the police service has become arguably the most successful institutional achievement of the wider peace process.

Changes included a new name, badge, and an extraordinarily expensive voluntary severance scheme (costing roughly £500 million) . A time-limited recruitment strategy involved the appointment of new officers on a controversial 50% Catholic and 50% “other” basis.

Undoubtedly, the organisation has transformed from its RUC inheritance. At the time of writing, about 31% of police officers are Catholic.

Evidence shows 91.5% of people in Northern Ireland feel safe in their community. And nearly three-quarters view the PSNI as effective in keeping areas safe. Around 92% of respondents felt confident contacting the PSNI if needed, and roughly 65% feel the police service represents their community. But importantly, unionists had more confidence in policing (73.8%) and nationalists less so (58.2%). The force also enjoys the backing of all political parties in Northern Ireland.

But policing is still buffeted by politics, both present and past and lower confidence among nationalists is indicative of concerns that remain 25 years after the Patten commission. A series of internal and external controversies have exacerbated this.

The resignation of PSNI chief constable Simon Byrne in 2023 was the result of a contentious and difficult series of events around the policing of a Troubles commemoration during a COVID lockdown. The organisation came as close as it ever has to being in complete crisis. The legacy of the past, concerns in the present and the still-divided Northern Irish community have all played a part.

In addition, Catholic applications are dropping precipitately and some political parties are calling for a “Patten II” amid concerns that the organisation has lost its way.

While the PSNI has been hoping for an application rate of around 50% from Catholics, only 26.7% of applications in a recent recruitment drive were from Catholics. As one young Catholic woman commented wryly during my research: “Sure, that’s not even a pass mark.”

My research with Jess Bonnan-White suggests several ongoing issues. They are organisational, rather than political. The most significant is its relationship – organisationally, historically and psychologically – with its RUC past.

Transformation and challenges

The incorporation of the RUC into the PSNI was a substantive issue when the service was created in 2001. Those who held an affinity to the RUC had argued for the preservation of its legacy. One outcome was that the RUC name was incorporated into the title deeds of the PSNI.

Transformation was obvious in the outward-facing sense – changes to the force’s name, symbols and uniform. But the RUC culture was preserved in the material reality of the police estate, commemorative medals, artefacts in the Newforge sports complex (which is still home to the RUC Athletic Association ), and the norms and attitudes within the service.

It is perhaps the culture in which the past is most evident. As former PSNI chief constable George Hamilton said in 2019: “Around 80% of the current police service were never in the RUC, but when you … see the photographs on the walls, when you listen to the stories in the police canteen, you’d think it was the opposite.”

This pairing of outward change and internal continuity has created an inherent tension and a cultural confusion. At times, this has actively hampered the service’s transformation.

Additionally, high-profile inquiries, including into atrocities such as the 1992 Sean Graham bookmaker shop murders , and accusations of RUC collusion, have dogged the PSNI. As the RUC was incorporated into the establishment of the PSNI, it has been difficult to fully separate the old from the new.

Where are we now?

Since it was established, the PSNI has lost two officers to dissident republican violence . It is fortunate not to have lost more. Our research suggests that the murders of Catholic officers Stephen Carroll and Ronan Kerr , and incidents that were foiled have fundamentally altered the trajectory of how “policing with the community” can be implemented.

In returning to a security mindset, the PSNI has been unable to integrate itself authentically into both communities, as envisaged by the Patten reforms. Such attacks have also acted as a major disincentive to Catholic recruits, exacerbating the challenge within the nationalist community.

A culture of fear internally and wariness externally have been compounded by organisational mistakes, such as the enormous 2023 data leak , which saw the names and roles of all staff briefly disclosed online.

For Catholics, policing can still mean alienation from their communities and families. There are also significant concerns internally about psychological safety – and worries that Catholic officers do not feel protected by the organisation.

Other fears – concerns around promotion and advancement, evidence of greater referrals of Catholic officers to professional standards, perceived inadequate transmission of intelligence to allow officers to keep themselves safe, as well as other forms of sectarianism – have come up in my discussions with officers .

Undoubtedly, the organisation faces significant structural problems. Brutal funding cuts, low officer numbers and a policing environment that is still volatile have all reduced the appetite for risk. While some of these challenges are common to policing in both Great Britain and the Irish Republic, the PSNI’s own research suggests that it has been hit much harder by financial cuts than comparative forces.

Despite these challenges, the PSNI has proved extraordinarily resilient. Ironically, the elements that underpinned this resilience – structures, history and organisational memory – have also been why it has struggled to build and maintain the confidence of the Catholic community.

The PSNI may have transformed from its RUC past, but it is still policing a divided society.

stories.body:
Imagine scrolling through social media and seeing dramatic weight-loss results from people taking Mounjaro, Wegovy or Ozempic. They share photographs, discuss side effects and recommend ways to get the best results.

These personal stories can feel convincing, especially when they come from people with similar experiences. For someone struggling with their weight , advice from a supportive online community may seem more relatable than information from a medical professional.

A 2026 UK study involving 684 adults, including 544 current or former users of weight-loss medications, found that 48% of participants used social media as a source of information about the drugs. Healthcare professionals were consulted less frequently.

Although the survey cannot tell us how widespread this behaviour is across the UK, it raises an interesting question: why might people trust advice from strangers online, even when medical professionals can offer more reliable information?

Psychology offers some clues.

Why personal stories carry so much weight

People are often more receptive to advice from those they see as members of their own group. Psychologists call this social identity : the sense of identity we gain from belonging to groups with shared experiences, interests or goals.

When someone identifies strongly with a group, they may pay particular attention to what other members say and do. Advice from people who share their experiences can feel more relevant and trustworthy, even when those people have no medical expertise.

For someone who has experienced judgement about their weight, finding people who understand their difficulties can be especially valuable.

In research I co-authored , we explored how a shared sense of identity could be encouraged in a group-based exercise rehabilitation programme for people with chronic lung disease. Although we did not test whether this improved outcomes, the work illustrated how a sense of belonging might encourage mutual support.

Similar psychological processes may help explain the appeal of online weight-loss communities.

The difficulty arises when trust in someone with shared experiences extends to their medical advice. A person may genuinely have benefited from a medication without understanding its risks or whether their experience is typical.

How online groups shape what people believe

Online communities can provide encouragement and practical support, but they can also influence which experiences receive attention and which opinions become widely accepted.

A 2021 study involving interviews with 32 people in a professionally supervised online weight-management programme in China found that peer support encouraged motivation and a sense of belonging. However, comparisons with other members could also reinforce unhelpful group expectations.

Similar pressures may arise in online communities discussing weight-loss medication.

For example, someone who repeatedly sees dramatic success stories may begin to expect the same results from their own treatment. If a particular medication is widely praised, questioning its effectiveness or discussing negative experiences might feel uncomfortable.

These influences do not affect everyone in the same way, but they help explain how advice can become accepted within a group, even when there is limited medical evidence to support it.

And the information circulating online is not always reliable.

An October 2026 study examined 194 popular TikTok and YouTube Shorts videos about weight-loss medications, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, the active ingredients in Wegovy and Mounjaro.

Only 24% of all views of the assessed videos were for content researchers judged to be medically accurate. Some videos contained incorrect medical information, while others provided too little clinical information to assess their accuracy.

The researchers examined a selected group of popular videos, so their findings cannot be generalised to everything shared about weight-loss drugs online.

Nevertheless, the findings illustrate how a video can attract considerable attention without providing the information someone needs to make a safe medical decision.

The risks of unregulated weight-loss drugs

The consequences can become more serious when online recommendations move beyond sharing experiences of prescribed medicines to encouraging people to obtain drugs that have not been approved for medical use.

One example is “Reta”, the nickname for retatrutide, an experimental weight-loss medication being developed by pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly.

Retatrutide has produced substantial weight loss in clinical trials , but it has not been authorised for medical use in the UK. Its benefits and risks are still being assessed.

Despite this, products marketed as “Reta” have been supplied through unregulated channels.

In October 2026, the UK medicines regulator seized more than 12,000 counterfeit weight-loss injection pens labelled as retatrutide or tirzepatide from a Birmingham industrial unit.

Products supplied through these channels may contain incorrect ingredients, unreliable doses or harmful contaminants.

There is an important distinction between these products and regulated prescription medicines. Mounjaro and Wegovy are authorised for weight management in the UK when prescribed appropriately. Ozempic contains semaglutide, the same active ingredient as Wegovy, but is licensed for treating type 2 diabetes.

Even approved medicines can cause side effects and require appropriate medical assessment.

A personal recommendation, however convincing, cannot establish whether an unregulated product is genuine or safe.

Making better-informed decisions

Online weight-loss communities can provide valuable emotional support, particularly for people who feel isolated or judged. The challenge is recognising when shared experiences begin to influence decisions that require medical expertise.

Before following advice about weight-loss medication, consider whether the person recommending it is promoting a product or receiving payment. Be particularly wary of dramatic promises, suggestions to change prescribed doses without medical advice or offers to supply medication outside regulated pharmacies.

It is also worth considering whether an online community welcomes discussion of side effects and disappointing experiences, or predominantly celebrates positive results. Groups that allow people to question claims may provide a more balanced picture.

Anyone considering weight-loss medication should seek advice from a qualified healthcare professional. The UK medicines regulator advises obtaining these medicines only with a valid prescription from a registered pharmacy.

Understanding how group identity influences trust can help people recognise the value of online support while being more critical of the medical advice they encounter.

Shared experiences can offer reassurance and encouragement, but decisions about medication should be informed by reliable evidence and individual medical advice.

stories.title: We Can’t Predict What Will Happen on Election Day. But We’ll Be Here to Cover It.
stories.summary: The post We Can’t Predict What Will Happen on Election Day. But We’ll Be Here to Cover It. appeared first on ProPublica .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.imageAlt: A row of people stand in white voting booths, with only their legs showing.
stories.body:
A Closer Look

Over the past year, we’ve tried to use the techniques of accountability journalism to add new facts to this pivotal moment in American history. We’ll keep that focus on Election Day — and beyond.

This has been a midterm election cycle unlike any other. Wealthy donors spent staggering sums . Both parties moved to redraw congressional district lines . President Donald Trump and his allies relentlessly questioned whether the results could be trusted even before a single ballot was counted. At Trump’s direction, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit that said the federal government would contest any outcome in which Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent in Alaska, was not victorious.

Newsrooms, including ours, have tried to plan how we will cover an election in which the losing side refuses to accept the will of the voters. Was the Alaska lawsuit a single data point or a harbinger?

As we prepare to write about Nov. 3 and beyond, we find ourselves in the uncomfortable position of trying to game out what might happen in the future — not our strong suit. The record shows that journalists are pretty good at telling readers what happened, particularly if we have some time and some data to sift through, and much less good at forecasting the future.

Help Us Report on Key Election Issues

ProPublica’s reporters are on the lookout for what’s going right and what isn’t. We’re monitoring voter suppression and interference, election observers and poll watchers, extremism tied to the election, and ICE activity at the polls. Have you seen something?

And yet we have to plan. Over the past few weeks we have prepared our reporters and editors to cover every scenario we can imagine. None of us have forgotten the chaos of 2020 when Trump was urged by advisers to send the military to seize voting machines in states he had lost. The Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol as lawmakers gathered to certify Joe Biden’s victory underscored the sense that literally anything was possible in the aftermath of elections.

We will have reporters on the ground in 11 key states covering voting, with even more in Washington, D.C., and others on standby. Our reporters have detailed what experts will be watching . But elections are no longer confined to Election Day (early voting and voting by mail constitute a huge share of the electorate). And our plans for covering voting stretch back many months.

Over the past year, we’ve tried to use the techniques of accountability journalism to add new facts to this pivotal moment in American history.

We have focused considerable attention on the mechanics of elections, a once-arcane issue that has become a central aspect of the MAGA movement’s argument that Trump’s 2020 loss was “rigged” by his opponents. We examined how the Trump administration depleted the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency , the arm of the federal government charged with safeguarding election systems. We discovered that Department of Homeland Security officials had asked CISA to obtain a voting machine and hack it without informing the manufacturer of any vulnerabilities found. The plan wasn’t acted on, but its existence made CISA employees fear they were being asked to take part in political interference. CISA and DHS didn’t respond to our questions, but a White House spokesperson said Trump “has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections.”

Another story looked at how delays resulting from the U.S. Postal Service’s cost-cutting measures endangered the validity of mail-in ballots in rural counties , typically Republican strongholds, during this year’s primaries. The Postal Service said such delays are less likely in the general election.

One of our most detailed election stories traced the career of Cleta Mitchell , a lawyer who spearheaded the legal attacks on the 2020 results. Mitchell leads a coalition of what she calls “election believers” — people who scour the voting results for errors that they believe point to larger conspiracies. Changes she’d hoped Trump could push through before the midterms, such as compelling states to turn over confidential voter information to the Justice Department, have been blocked by the courts . But she has nonetheless become the voice of a well-funded national movement, one which has the president’s ear. When Trump is weighing what to do in the aftermath of this week’s vote, our reporting strongly suggests that Mitchell will be among the people he listens to.

We asked to speak with Mitchell multiple times. She declined but told us in an email: “​​​​What we focus on is making sure the election process is accurate, transparent, and honest. The ONLY steps I’ve urged the Administration to take are those that will give the voters — ALL voters — confidence that the outcomes are correct.” A White House spokesperson said she has no official role in election policy but is an effective private advocate.

We have also spent time doing the traditional work of investigative reporting, looking closely at candidates’ records in public office. A newsroom like ours can’t cover every race, so we focus our resources on areas where we have particular expertise.

Our team in Texas has covered state Attorney General Ken Paxton for years, and we kept our focus once he announced he would run for the U.S. Senate. One story looked at his travels, revealing that only 1 in 6 of his nearly 1,000 out-of-state trips were linked to his official duties. Texas taxpayers paid $3.3 million for Paxton’s security detail to accompany him. (Paxton didn’t answer our questions, but his office said he “faced numerous security threats.”) That has become an issue in the Senate campaign.

Another opportunity arose from an investigation that was seemingly not related to the midterms: our examination of the Trump administration’s handling of the Justice Department. We began many months ago to look for promising cases that had been dropped and found out the FBI had been looking into pay-to-play allegations involving prominent Democratic and Republican members of Congress. The case included a bipartisan list of political figures such as Susan Collins , the Republican senator from Maine running in a closely contested race this year, and James Clyburn , a leading Democratic representative from South Carolina who’s also on the ballot this year.

Our first story revealed that Collins helped a little-known defense contractor win millions in federal contracts while the company’s CEO helped bankroll her 2020 reelection effort through a donation made via a shell company. Our second story revealed that the FBI was looking into interactions that Clyburn and Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died in July, had with the same contractor. Collins has denied all wrongdoing. “A donation would never cause Congressman Clyburn to increase his support for the donor’s request,” Clyburn’s office said. Graham’s communications director wrote that “any allegations of quid-pro-quo behavior … are simply false.” The FBI stopped examining the allegations after Trump purged the bureau. Our coverage likewise has become an issue in the Maine race.

We stand at a moment of uncertainty in our history as a democracy. Trump has made his willingness to smear news organizations an essential aspect of his appeal. He routinely insults reporters to their face and has attempted to ban some outlets from the White House and Air Force One because he didn’t like the stories they wrote about him. He has diverted hundreds of federal agents from their jobs fighting drug cartels and organized crime to search for evidence that noncitizens have illegally voted in federal elections. Hardly any were found .

I’m deeply reluctant to make any predictions about how all this will end. ProPublica prepared for an array of dire scenarios in November of 2024 that might arise from a close election. None of them came to pass as Trump decisively prevailed. A federal judge dismissed the Justice Department’s lawsuit to block the Alaska Senate race results over the weekend, and the Trump administration’s plans to appeal stand on shaky legal ground.

The one thing I know for certain is that we will keep digging into the story of what really happened in this election, whoever wins.

stories.title: I Was There to Document the Aftermath of Deadly Flooding. Then, It Started Raining.
stories.summary: The post I Was There to Document the Aftermath of Deadly Flooding. Then, It Started Raining. appeared first on ProPublica .

stories.imageAlt: Sunlight reflects off a calm, shallow stream winding through a quiet, shaded woodland area flanked by trees and exposed roots.
stories.body:
Three people died in Ruidoso, New Mexico, last year when floods swept through the area. As the mayor prioritized tourism after the flood recovery, first responders said they weren’t equipped. Our visual journalist documented the unfolding story.

Three summers ago, over Father’s Day weekend, my family and I went camping in the Lincoln National Forest, just a few hours drive north of our home in El Paso, Texas. It’s a beautiful area that’s long served as a getaway for the region, with skiing in the winter, and golf and hiking in the summer. My daughter played under the trees, and I rode my bike down mountain trails that, I noticed, seemed concerningly dry.

The next evening, after we left to drive home, two fires started in forests surrounding the town of Ruidoso, New Mexico, around 25 miles away from where we’d been. I watched horrifying videos online of fire lapping the mountains behind the village’s strip malls and parking lots. The fires were eventually suppressed by a combination of human effort and the late summer monsoon season. But when the downpour of rain hit the burnt landscape around Ruidoso, it created another problem: Recurring floods then ripped through town, damaging homes and infrastructure, and leading to emergency rescues.

The following summer, the scene repeated. On July 8, 2025, monsoon rain hit a burn scar and quickly swelled the Rio Ruidoso and its tributaries. Three people — two of them children — lost their lives.

Reporter Abe Streep, a member of ProPublica’s Southwest office, and I met in Ruidoso to report on what happened. Ruidoso is a place built on tourism, with a paid (rather than volunteer) fire department staff and its own disaster manager. How could two children and a man be swept to their deaths in a place that appeared equipped to handle such disasters?

In two stories ProPublica recently published, Abe answered those questions. He found that, after the 2024 fires, experts warned the town of increased flash flooding risks . Initially, local and state leaders considered a relocation plan for some homes and businesses that would get people out of harm’s way, but the project faltered. Instead, village leaders continued promoting tourism to the town, and the mayor even chastised residents for warning of floods on social media. Abe also reported that, while local and state officials insisted the emergency response to the flood was admirable, first responders say the three deaths could have been avoided . The responders told Abe that village leadership left them understaffed and inadequately equipped to contend with the flooding.

The Village of Ruidoso did not respond to detailed written questions about its emergency response, and it has not publicly released a report on rescue efforts during the flood. Reached by phone, the fire chief, Cade Hall, disputed our reporting but declined to provide specifics. Mayor Lynn Crawford has said protecting the village includes balancing public safety with tourism, the lifeblood of its economy. But in an interview last year, Crawford said to Abe and me: “Who’s to blame? I didn’t start the fire.”

My role as a photographer was to document Ruidoso as the story unfolded — to visualize the people and place at the center of it. It’s a role I’ve had countless times in my career, but this story hit unexpectedly close to home. I could imagine my own family caught unaware in a similar situation, trying to escape the El Paso summer heat but instead navigating an unfathomable disaster.

When Abe and I started reporting, we met people from the community and out of town who tried to help. I watched as New Mexico National Guard service members loaded sand bags into families’ cars, people prepared hot meals for those who had been displaced and volunteers handed out donated supplies from collection centers.

While we were reporting one afternoon, it started raining. Fear swept through me. Our phones lit up with flood warnings from the National Weather Service. We knew we should take them seriously.

Abe and I sought refuge in a local brewery perched high above the river basin. Before we knew it, the water from that thin little creek of Rio Ruidoso became a torrent. The rushing water rose quickly. It swept through the river valley right under the brewery, carrying what looked like trees and debris with it.

Still, I wanted to photograph the river up close. I left the safety of the brewery and let the heavy rain cover me as I moved closer to the river. As I made photos that afternoon and throughout the rest of the trip, questions about my own safety ran through my mind: Would the water keep rising? If it did, could I get to high ground? And, notably, would I have enough warning?

In hindsight, I realize these questions were largely about whether I could trust the systems in place to keep me and others safe. And as Abe kept reporting over the next year, the more those questions felt valid.

Last month, Abe and I traveled again to Ruidoso. The town felt lighter and less ominous. Much of the ruin had been removed or rebuilt. Grass and sagebrush sprouted on a burn scar. Tourists wandered around a lively downtown on a Friday afternoon. People seemed to be moving on from the terror of the previous year.

But Stephanie and Sebastian Trotter still carry the scars of the day. They lost their two children, Sebastian Rowan, 7, and Charlotte, 4, in the Ruidoso flooding.

There is now a memorial for them and Benjamin “Tim” Feagin, the third person who died, at the RV park where they had been camped. But I wanted to see for myself the places where each of them was found. I felt that making photos of those places could help people connect with the reality of their deaths as well as their lives. So, early one morning, I walked along the floodplain trying to find the locations Abe had shared with me.

I got to the bridge where a firefighter found Sebastian Rowan. There was no marker, no indication that anyone’s body had been found there.

Then I went looking for the area where Charlotte was found. I wandered under pine and cottonwood, through knee-deep grasses and wild sunflowers. Crows cawed overhead, and the early morning sun broke through the trees. I stood there for a while, admiring the beauty, awed by the sadness of the river’s trickle.

stories.title: Bankrolling American Empire in the Philippines
stories.summary: The Pentagon and private capital have teamed up to militarize the island nation. The post Bankrolling American Empire in the Philippines appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Subic Bay (Shutterstock)

Originally published in TomDispatch .

During the Cold War, the Subic Bay Naval Base in the Philippines was a key enabler of U.S. military operations in the Pacific and beyond. It served as a critical support facility for the U.S. war in Vietnam and a transit point for U.S. weapons destined for American military personnel in the 1991 Persian Gulf War. That all changed in June of that year, when the Philippine Congress, under pressure from a grassroots anti-bases movement, refused to renew the lease for Subic Bay and other U.S. outposts in that nation.

After the closing of U.S. bases, military relations between the U.S. and the Philippines were conducted indirectly through arms transfers, joint training exercises, and deployments of Special Operations forces to aid Philippine counterinsurgency efforts, rather than by the permanent presence of tens of thousands of troops. The relationship was codified in 1999, when Washington and Manila entered into a Visiting Forces Agreement , which eased the movement of U.S. troops and equipment in and out of the Philippines and put U.S. personnel in the country under the jurisdiction of U.S. rather than Philippine authorities.

But now Subic Bay is back in play as part of a new expansion of the U.S. military presence in the Philippines. And this time around, private capital is financing these empire games.

Military Might Versus Human Rights

The long-standing U.S. military ties with the Philippines have come at a high price for the residents of that nation. Washington’s military and economic interests there have prompted it to look the other way as repressive leaders like Ferdinand Marcos and Rodrigo Duterte engaged in systematic human rights abuses against their own people.

To its credit, the Reagan administration eventually cut ties with Marcos — who was overthrown through peaceful protests known as the “People Power” revolt in 1986 — throwing its support behind his democratically elected opponent, Corazon Aquino. But there was no such shift with respect to Duterte, whose regime ruled the Philippines from 2016 to 2022, and engaged in extrajudicial killings of thousands of Filipinos, including journalists and land reform activists, all under the guise of a “ war on drugs .” Duterte is now under indictment by the International Criminal Court, which has cited him for “the crimes against humanity of murder and attempted murder.”

While Marcos and his family fled the Philippines in the 1980s, his son — Ferdinand Marcos Jr. — returned and, in 2022, won the presidency in a landslide , in part by promising to continue some of the strongman policies introduced by Duterte. According to Human Rights Watch , since the younger Marcos took office:

Serious human rights violations have continued in the country largely unabated, including arbitrary arrests, extrajudicial killings and enforced disappearances by security forces. The murderous ‘war on drugs’ has continued, though with fewer killings. Leftist civil society activists, journalists, environmentalists, Indigenous leaders, trade unionists, and left-wing politicians remain under serious, at times deadly, threat.

During the Biden presidency, the U.S. expanded a 2014 pact — the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement — which gave the U.S. military access to five major sites in the Philippines. In 2023, the number of bases was expanded to nine . The State Department has described the scope of the EDCA as authorizing “U.S. forces access to agreed locations in the Philippines on a rotational basis, for security cooperation exercises, joint and combined military training activities, and humanitarian assistance and disaster relief activities.” That official summary fails to admit the real reason for the signing of the EDCA: to give the U.S. access to territory that can be used in a future war with China.

The Privatization of Subic Bay

Building on his predecessor’s enhanced cooperation with the Philippines, President Donald Trump, who had been a staunch Duterte supporter , has pursued even tighter ties with Marcos’s government. This has been driven, in significant part, by the desire to use the Philippines as a platform for potential U.S. military interventions in the Pacific region and further economic penetration of Asia.

As part of the accelerating security partnership between the U.S. and the Philippines, military activities at Subic Bay have resumed. But this time, formal access has been secured by a private investment firm, Cerberus Capital Management , which controls the area through a 50-year lease granted through collaboration with a Philippine company, Agila.

A report by the New York Committee for Human Rights in the Philippines, a member of the International Coalition for Human Rights in the Philippines, summarized current activities at Subic Bay:

In mid-2025, the U.S. Congress approved a plan to build a forward operating base and ammunition production facility in Subic Bay. It is projected to be the world’s largest weapons hub. … The shipyard [is home to] HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, deep sea fiber optic data cables manufacturer Sub Com, defense contractor V2X and the Philippine Navy, which operates a portion of the facility.

Cerberus has strong ties to the Trump administration, first and foremost through its founder, Stephen Feinberg , who is deputy secretary of the Department of War, second in command at the Pentagon behind Pete Hegseth. In that role, Feinberg oversees the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital, which makes loans to military tech companies, many of which are current or former Cerberus clients.

Feinberg “earned” his position the old-fashioned way — by giving millions to Rebuilding America Now, a super PAC devoted to supporting Trump, and hosting a $50,000-a-plate fundraiser, the proceeds of which also went to support candidate Trump in 2016.

Bloomberg News has identified four other former Cerberus executives now in key positions at the Pentagon: David Lorch, director of the OSC; George Kollitides, a special government employee who is simultaneously a director of D. Boral Acquisition, a company that brokers mergers and acquisitions in the weapons sector; and senior Pentagon advisers John Gallagher and Tom Rakusan.

On the other side of the revolving door, Cerberus has hired major Republican figures like former Treasury Secretary John Snow and former Vice President Dan Quayle, who serves as chair of the company’s global investment unit. Given these connections, the Pentagon is all-in behind Cerberus’s activities in the Philippines. But this has prompted a backlash. Activists in the Philippines and beyond are speaking out against the role of Cerberus, calling for public pension funds to withdraw their investments in the company for underwriting the militarization of the Philippines.

Another important avenue of increased cooperation between the U.S. and the Marcos government is the Philippines’ participation in Pax Silica , a U.S.-initiated cartel that the State Department describes as its “flagship effort on AI and supply chain security, advancing new economic security consensus among allies and trusted partners.” And by “supply chain security,” the declaration primarily means “reducing dependence on China” for critical minerals needed to feed and sustain the computing power now central to the Pentagon and the U.S. arms industry.

In addition to the Philippines, there are 24 other participants in Pax Silica, including two other key Asian partners, India and Japan, as well as Taiwan, which is an associate member of the cartel. Jacob Helberg, a former adviser to military tech giant Palantir who now serves as the State Department’s point person on Pax Silica, has stressed that the initiative goes well beyond just securing the supply of specific critical resources. “If the 20th century ran on oil and steel, the 21st century runs on [computing power] and the minerals that feed it,” he said. “This declaration [announcing Pax Silica] hails a new economic security consensus ensuring aligned partners build the AI ecosystem of tomorrow — from energy and critical minerals to high-end manufacturing models.”

The China Syndrome

Although it supplies many other benefits to U.S. corporations and America’s national security state, the enhanced effort to bring the Philippines more securely into the U.S. military, political and economic orbit is all rationalized as moves toward reining in China’s economic and military power and garnering Manila’s support in a possible war between China and the U.S.

The policy of economic warfare and aggressively preparing for a military conflict with China could not be more misguided. The oft-cited “need” to posture U.S. forces to do battle with China over Taiwan ignores the fact that there are diplomatic means of preventing such a conflict.

What is needed is a joint understanding on the status of Taiwan. For over 40 years, peace in the Taiwan Strait has been maintained through the U.S.–China agreement that Washington will not take steps toward recognizing Taiwan as an independent state and China would agree not to resolve the issue of Taiwan by force — the so-called “One China” policy. That agreement has been weakened by actions taken during both the Biden and Trump administrations. The simplest and best way for Washington and Beijing to avoid a war over Taiwan would be to revert to the “One China” policy.

Using trade wars and military buildups as the primary U.S. tool for influencing China simply will not work.

China does not pose a direct military threat to the United States. Its last major war was its invasion of Vietnam in 1979, a conflict in which its troops were badly beaten by battle-hardened Vietnamese forces. The U.S. also spends almost three times as much on its military as China does, and is far ahead of Beijing in numbers of advanced combat aircraft, naval firepower, and nuclear weapons.

In areas where China might be a peer competitor with the U.S. military, like AI-driven weapons , there need to be some rules of the road on how such systems can be used. Using trade wars and military buildups as the primary U.S. tool for influencing China simply will not work. The likely result of persisting in such an approach will be a dangerous arms race and an increased risk of outright war.

A more productive approach to U.S.–China relations would be to seriously explore cooperation on central issues like arms control, addressing the climate crisis, and stabilizing the global economy. There would still be a U.S. military strategy for the Asia–Pacific region, but it should be genuinely defensive in nature, a posture that could save hundreds of billions of dollars in the years to come.

Pursuing a more balanced policy toward China would open the way to developing more equal, less exploitative relations with the Philippines and other nations in the Pacific , and it would allow Washington to finally take a genuine interest in promoting human rights and opposing repression as central pillars of U.S. international relations.

At a time when armed conflict and threats of war are the bedrock of U.S. policy, from the Western Hemisphere to the Middle East, a shift toward diplomacy seems daunting . But it is the only way forward if we want to move toward a more peaceful world where no one nation or group of nations dominates, and where corporations aren’t bending foreign and domestic policies to their will.

stories.title: Washington’s War, Beijing’s Tanks
stories.summary: China is absorbing the shock of the Iran War for the rest of Asia. The post Washington’s War, Beijing’s Tanks appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sinopec oil storage tanks in Wuhan, China (Shutterstock)

Donald Trump insists that oil is moving through the Strait of Hormuz above pre-war levels. Brent crude settled at $117.38 on Friday and was still trading near $114 on Monday, a day after Qatari mediators arrived in Tehran to head off the next round of fighting. The market heard the president and kept bidding.

It has cause. The U.S.-Israeli war on Iran is in its ninth month, and October has been its worst month yet for shipping. At least 12 ships were attacked in and around the strait in the week ending October 16, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations. Energy Secretary Chris Wright says that Gulf crude flows are back to 80-90 percent of pre-war levels; Kpler’s tracking put September’s Hormuz exports at about 44 percent of February’s. Washington and Tehran have both drawn up plans to resume the wider war, possibly after Americans vote on November 3.

The bill has not been split evenly. The International Monetary Fund now assumes that Hormuz traffic will not resume until March 2027, and it has warned that poorer economies dependent on imported oil are the most exposed. It cut its 2026 forecast for the Philippines, which draws 95 percent of its crude imports from the Middle East, to 3.4 percent from 5.6 percent in January. Fuel subsidies have widened budget deficits in Indonesia and Malaysia. Americans are paying as well: diesel has climbed about 70 percent in a year, to $6.28 a gallon .

Washington’s response has run to naval escorts, threats of more bombing, a sanctions waiver for Russian diesel, and appeals to European governments to release their own diesel stocks. Washington has also relied on China to absorb a large share of the shock.

China imported a record 11.6 million barrels a day in 2025, filling storage while crude was at its cheapest since 2020. When the strait closed, Chinese refiners stopped chasing every cargo and ran down what they had banked. Second-quarter imports fell 32 percent from the first quarter, to 8.1 million barrels a day. In September they were 21.5 percent lower than a year earlier, and onshore crude stocks fell by 57 million barrels in the month on Vortexa’s count, the largest monthly draw in analysts’ records.

Beijing’s motive was commercial. Refiners facing $100 crude and thin margins had every reason to burn stock instead of buying. The effect spread well beyond China. The U.S. Energy Information Administration found that weaker Chinese buying reduced global demand and softened the price impact of the lost supply. Société Générale ranked the pullback among the largest offsets to the shock, behind only Saudi Arabia’s rerouting and ahead of the coordinated reserve releases by the United States, Europe, and Japan.

Western strategic reserves exist to steady markets in exactly this kind of emergency. China’s tanks, filled for China’s own security, did more of that work.

The neighbors felt it most. Kpler has described China as the oil market’s main balancing mechanism, and more than half of Southeast Asia’s crude imports come from the Middle East. Every cargo Chinese refiners passed up was one fewer bid against Manila or Hanoi in the spot market.

China kept buying, just not crude. Customs data show its imports grew 22.3 percent in yuan terms in the first nine months, faster than its exports, and September imports rose 31 percent in dollar terms. Some of that is price. For suppliers across Asia, China remained a growing customer in a year when their own fuel bills were climbing.

The cushion is not bottomless. Fuel is where it has worn thinnest: Chinese diesel and gasoline inventories fell in September to their lowest in more than a decade as refiners shipped product abroad. Beijing held back October export approvals over its Golden Week holiday, then resumed fuel exports , a step Reuters said would ease tight global fuel markets. Approvals now come month by month.

Crude is less stretched than it looks. A Reuters calculation shows that China drew on stocks in four of the past five months, yet heavy buying before the war leaves it with a small surplus for the first three quarters and a stockpile of at least 1.2 billion barrels. Imports are edging up again, and Kpler expects seaborne arrivals of 8-8.5 million barrels a day this quarter. If refiners rush back to refill at $115, China stops being Asia’s cushion and becomes one more bidder.

Beijing has a second buffer it has barely used: its own households. Third-quarter growth of 4.5 percent leaned on factories. Exports jumped 36.3 percent in September, while consumer prices rose just 0.9 percent and property investment fell 20.6 percent over nine months. Europe’s deficit with China hit a record $34.8 billion in September, and Ursula von der Leyen says that the European Commission is building an instrument, due in December, that could restrict the access of some Chinese goods to the single market.

Chinese households might be able to carry more. Retail sales rose 1.1 percent in September against a forecast of 0.5 percent; excluding cars they grew 3.9 percent , the fastest since October 2025. China’s top economic planner pledged on October 20 to expand domestic demand with greater force. December’s Central Economic Work Conference will show whether that means bigger rural pensions and health coverage that follows migrant workers into the cities, or another round of infrastructure that adds to the very output Brussels is counting.

Washington’s part is simpler. No stockpile, Chinese or American, substitutes for a settlement that lets tankers through without being shot at. The IMF has penciled in a closed strait until March 2027. Every month a deal arrives before then is a month Asia stops paying for a war it did not start.

November’s customs and retail figures will show which China Asia is dealing with this winter. If crude imports stay restrained while shoppers keep accelerating, the region gets a second cushion, made of Chinese demand rather than Chinese storage. If the tanks refill first and the shoppers stall, Asia loses the first cushion without gaining the second.

The strait will reopen on terms settled between Washington and Tehran. How much of the bill Asia pays until then is still being decided in Beijing.

stories.title: The Sediment Of Culture Shapes Political Order
stories.summary: The post The Sediment Of Culture Shapes Political Order appeared first on NOEMA .

stories.body:
Governing systems are effective when power, ideology and deep culture are aligned.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

As a global journal of ideas, Noema receives feedback from readers all over the world that broadens our way of seeing and kindles the further iteration of our thinking. One recent case is a response by Carl Gay, an executive of the Cloudspago consultancy in Australia, to the Noema essay “When The Present Eats The Future: The Achilles Heel of Consumer Democracies.”

In that essay, I contrast post-Mao China’s capacity for reaching a consensus on long-term goals and determinedly implementing them over many years without a break in continuity with the increasing inability of consumer democracies to do so. The example I used in the context of climate change was how China set the goal decades ago of dominating green technology, especially electric vehicles and batteries, and has steadily achieved that objective, while most open societies of the West have sputtered behind. Its “whole dragon” approach brings the resources of the entire system to bear on the challenge at hand.

I pointed out that the strength of China’s system is closely related to its chief flaw: enforcing order and repressing freedom to keep the consensus from fraying. In his note to Noema, Gay makes explicit what I only implied: To the extent China’s determined continuity clogs corrective feedback loops, a policy ordained by the Party can go off in the wrong direction for a very long time, causing damage not easily repaired.

The example he uses is the disastrous one-child policy that held from 1980-2015. It resulted in today’s demographic implosion, where there are not enough young people to sustain the welfare of an aging society. Indeed, blinkered assumptions from the present, projected forward, robbed the future of a balanced population.

Another less calamitous case in point was the 2022 COVID lockdown, which went on well past the patience of a restless public. In that case, the nascent feedback loops of contagious online rants, instances of journalistic exposure and even episodic outbursts of public demonstration resulted in a responsive and more immediate change in policy.

“Deep culture always returns to shape a society in a way similar to how a person’s emotional subconscious is forever biting at the heels of rational cognition.”

The Equivalent Of Market Signals In Politics

The big question for China’s one-party juggernaut is whether it can accommodate corrective feedback mechanisms in politics that are equivalent to the market signals it accommodates to check state-backed economic policy from going too far down the wrong path.

Two developments are emerging that impact this feedback deficit. Paradoxically, the first is that expanded surveillance from the top serves at the same time to register people’s dissatisfaction to the Party guardians listening at scale.

The other is that China’s densely wired society has become a ready platform for surveillance of official behavior from below, or sousveillance . Citizen reports, especially about corruption, rapidly gain virality when posted online.

This dual potential is not lost on the authorities. In a candid conversation in Beijing in 2015, China’s then cyber czar, Lu Wei, openly acknowledged that, in the absence of electoral accountability, an active netizenry can be a critical channel for sending rectifying signals from the grassroots to the Party hierarchy. Even the choice of keyword searches used to invoke censorship can be considered a form of feedback.

Needless to say, if the receiver is not attuned to the signal frequency, the message will go unheard. Read Noema in print.

Beyond that, a Shanghai entrepreneur I know who was a founder of YouKu, China’s version of YouTube, has told me how the Party is constantly polling down to the neighborhood level to gauge any discontent that may be bubbling up.

China scholar John Keane goes so far as to suggest that China is becoming a kind of “phantom democracy.” By that, he means “the fear of democracy forces a style of political management that in many ways mirrors and mimics electoral systems, where the fear of elections puts leaders in a constant campaign mode” as they feel the need to continually convince constituencies of their worthiness and legitimacy.

But Gay’s key insight in his reply to the Noema essay is more profound and is a larger frame for understanding why China functions as well as it does in contrast to consumer democracies.

“Culture is the substructure upon which the superstructure of ideology, politics and economics are built — the opposite of how modern thought would have it.”

Accumulated Culture Matters Most

As Gay puts it, “power, ideology and culture run at three speeds. Power changes in years, ideology in decades, culture in generations. China’s ‘whole dragon’ approach works because all three are aligned: a power layer that sets fifty-year goals, an ideology that makes its accountability internal and a culture with two thousand years of examination-system deference deposited in it. The continuity you admire is what alignment produces.

“Consumer democracies have the opposite shape: a return channel for error and no continuity. But ‘a governing consensus that sticks’ is a power-layer prescription, and consensus can’t be installed at the power layer when the culture isn’t carrying it. The rules change; the people don’t. Democracies lack a constituency for the future not because opinion is fickle but because the culture hasn’t yet accumulated the consequences that would create one. It will, when the damage becomes undeniable. That is slower than the climate clock allows, but it’s the only route the mechanism offers.”

Gay expanded on this useful frame elsewhere in an essay titled, “Power, Ideology And Culture: The Sediment Beneath Politics.”

“Political order is not one thing but three, moving at three different speeds,” Gay explains in his essay. “There is power — the hard architecture of institutions, coercion, money and command, the layer that can change in a season. There is ideology — the story a society tells about why those with power deserve it and why the rest should comply. And there is culture — the slow accumulation of everything a people has lived through, settled so deep that it is no longer argued but simply assumed. Most of our political commentary treats these as rival explanations: the institutionalist sees only power, the theorist only ideology, the culture critic only identity. Each is holding one limb of the animal.

“The reframe I would urge is this. Culture is not a third thing standing beside the other two. It is mostly the other two — power and ideology accumulated over generations and set hard, the way sediment is only the silt from yesteryear’s flood waters deposited over time, slowly compressing to a firmer sedimentary structure. What a people will accept, resist or demand today is the settled residue of the power arrangements and the justifying stories it absorbed long before anyone now living was old enough to question them. This is why culture is the slowest layer to move, and why, when it finally does move, power and ideology have no choice but to follow.”

Deep culture always returns to shape a society in a way similar to how a person’s emotional subconscious is forever biting at the heels of rational cognition. Culture is the substructure upon which the superstructure of ideology, politics and economics are built — the opposite of how modern thought would have it.

As political orders around the world enter a protracted period of upheaval, Gay’s frame of whether they are aligned or not with their cultural grounding is one of the more compelling paradigms for making sense of it all.

stories.body:
Low water levels on Lake Powell have revealed parts of Glen Canyon that were long submerged. Ted Wood

WATER

Lake Powell recently dropped to a historic low, slashing hydropower and the flow of water downstream. As drought deepens, groups are pushing to drain the lake entirely to reveal its long-submerged rock arches and spires and allow wildlife along the Colorado River to recover.

By Jim Robbins • October 29, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

The 27-year-long drought in the Southwestern U.S. — the longest dry period in the last 1,200 years — is taking a serious toll on the flow of the Colorado River. Climate change is shrinking the snowpack in Colorado’s Rocky Mountains, the source of roughly 80 percent of the river’s annual flow, and higher temperatures are melting the snowpack earlier in the year, which saps runoff in late summer and fall. Warmer weather is also increasing evaporation from the river’s 40 reservoirs, including its two largest — Lakes Powell and Mead.

Last month, Lake Powell, on the Utah-Arizona border, reached a record low, at less than 150 feet above dead pool, the point at which water can no longer flow through the Glen Canyon Dam’s bypass tubes to reach Lake Mead, behind Hoover Dam, 300 miles downstream. The low water levels reduced the generation of hydropower from both reservoirs, complicated how riverine ecosystems are managed, and slashed deliveries of water to the Lower Basin states of Arizona, California, and Nevada.

Farmers are fallowing fields. Developers in some areas have paused housing construction for lack of guaranteed water supplies. And the Bureau of Reclamation has curtailed its “environmental flows” — releases of cold water from Powell — which is threatening protected fish and preventing the buildup of sandbars that provide habitat for wildlife in the Grand Canyon. No matter how the river is managed going forward, observers say, ecosystems both downstream and up will see significant changes.

Faced with the prospect of even lower Colorado River levels, the federal and state governments have been scrambling to come up with ways to meet the competing demands of disparate interests that rely on its flow, from topping off Lake Powell with water diverted from upstream reservoirs, to slashing downstream water deliveries by 40 percent, to paying farmers to keep their allocations of water in the river. The crisis is even causing some to consider a fix once deemed unthinkable: draining Lake Powell entirely.

A map of Lake Mead and Lake Powell on the Colorado River. Yale Environment 360 / Created with Datawrapper

When the Glen Canyon Dam was built in the 1960s, proponents hyped its benefits: cheap hydropower, subsidized water for cotton and alfalfa growers, real estate on the new lakeshore, and a playground for boaters. But detractors bemoaned the drowning of Glen Canyon itself, a red rock labyrinth of gorges, spires, cliffs, and grottoes that conservationists described as even more beautiful than the Grand Canyon.

Over the decades, some environmental advocates have argued for removing the Glen Canyon Dam and restoring the canyon, but the idea was always dismissed as too expensive and, because it would wipe out power generation, wildly impractical.

Now, a more tempered approach is gaining support, with groups like the Glen Canyon Institute arguing not to remove the dam but to drain Lake Powell through new diversion tunnels that would be drilled below the existing bypass tubes, close to the riverbed. The upsides, say advocates, would be manifold. The water would boost hydropower production in Lake Mead. The stunning formations of Glen Canyon and sites sacred to Indigenous people would reemerge. Wildlife would return, and riparian habitat above and below the dam site would eventually be restored. The plan is called Fill Mead First.

For more than four decades, the Glen Canyon Dam was considered a huge asset to the river basin, said Eric Balken, executive director of the Glen Canyon Institute. But it’s now “becoming a liability because it might actually prevent water from flowing downstream. All of the core assumptions around the dam have been turned on their head.”

The Glen Canyon Dam. George Frey / Getty Images

That’s because of the dam’s structural limitations. If the lake drops below minimum power pool, its penstocks — the large pipes that send water to the dam’s eight turbines — will be left stranded, high and dry. Lake water will instead be released through bypass tubes, which sit below the penstocks but have less than half their capacity to discharge water.

These tubes were not built for sustained long-term use, and sending high volumes of water through them could cause vibrations, scouring, and other effects that could cause irreparable damage to the dam. While the Bureau of Reclamation has long warned about relying solely on the bypass tubes to release water, after inspecting and relining them in 2025 it said they might work if needed. But another challenge will remain: Relying on the narrow tubes will make it harder for Upper Basin states (Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) to meet their delivery obligations to Lower Basin states and, by international agreement, Mexico.

Allowing more water to flow through the Glen Canyon Dam — by draining the lake through the existing bypass tubes and newly drilled diversion tunnels near the riverbed — is no longer dismissed out of hand. “That conversation has evolved,” said Kathryn Sorensen, director of research at the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University.

A diagram of the Glen Canyon Dam. The minimum power pool is the lowest level at which it is possible to generate power. Dead pool is the point at which water stops flowing through the dam. Yale Environment 360

Lower release structures, said Jack Schmidt, director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University, are “an utterly reasonable idea” and should be part of the discussion. As for Powell’s potential loss of hydropower, proponents of dam removal say those megawatts could be replaced with solar power. The new Gemini solar plant near Las Vegas has a capacity of 690 megawatts; the Glen Canyon Dam currently has a capacity of around 730 megawatts.

The Lower Basin states, which primarily take their water from Lake Mead and are seeing their allotments held back to prop up Lake Powell, have urged the federal government to consider modifying the dam with lower outlets rather than cutting back on deliveries, as the Biden administration ordered in 2024.

“Addressing the infrastructure limitations may be the one long-term measure that would best achieve operation and management improvements to the Glen Canyon Dam,” representatives of the Lower Basin states wrote to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum last year.

Draining Lake Powell completely “could [annually] reduce evaporative losses by a couple hundred thousand acre-feet,” said Sorensen: Experts say 11 percent of the water in the reservoir is lost to evaporation each year. “On a river that is much smaller than anyone expected, that water really matters,” she said. But while the Glen Canyon Institute plan is gaining some traction, she added, “it faces a lot of obstacles.”

Boaters travel under Gregory Natural Bridge, in Lake Powell, which was under water until 2021. Francisco Kjolseth / The Salt Lake Tribune

One of those obstacles is the federal government, which did not even consider the possibility of draining Lake Powell as an option in its recent environmental impact statement — finalized in August — which addressed ways to manage the Colorado over the next 10 years.

Officials in Page, Arizona, which has a thriving water-based recreation industry, have also opposed draining the lake. The BlueRibbon Coalition, which represents off-road and motorized outdoor recreation, leads the opposition. It has put forward a model bill called the Colorado River Abundance Act, which would supply treated water to Lower Basin states, allowing more water to be retained in Lake Powell. The treated water would come from nuclear-powered desalination of seawater and briny water and through “advanced water reuse,” in which wastewater is cleaned with filter technologies, at an estimated cost of $40 billion.

Another obstacle is time: New diversion tunnels would likely take a decade to study, design, and build. And the price tag could be in the billions.

The Colorado’s reduced flows are, meanwhile, taking a toll on riverine ecosystems, which scientists call “novel” because they have been radically altered by 70 years of human activity — most significantly by the elimination of seasonal flooding. For a number of reasons, including low lake levels, the Bureau of Reclamation has canceled many environmental flows from the Glen Canyon Dam in recent years, depriving the Colorado of a large pulse of sediment, which is a part of the river’s natural ecology. The flows rebuild sandbars and beaches used by boaters in the Grand Canyon, and they create shallow-water habitat for threatened and endangered native fish.

Long-drowned cottonwood trees in Lake Powell have resurfaced as water levels have dropped. Carolyn Cole / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

The Bureau also occasionally releases cold water from the dam to lower the river’s temperature and keep invasive, warm-water-loving bass from taking up residence in the Grand Canyon stretch and displacing native fish. But because of the drought, which is already reducing hydroelectric production, those releases have also been curtailed.

Draining the lake completely would allow Glen Canyon to recover as the river flushes out built-up sediment, experts say. Native cottonwoods and willows would take root and help push out invasives, like tamarisk. River otters, beavers, birds, and amphibians would return to the canyon. And the drowned red rock arches, natural bridges, amphitheaters, and waterfalls would gradually emerge from the muck, along with thousands of sites sacred to Native Americans.

A shift in the hydrological regime would also have profound effects on hundreds of miles of river ecosystems below Glen Canyon Dam, including in the Grand Canyon. “It would change in ways that are only partially predictable,” said Schmidt. “Suddenly the river would have great fluctuations. The river would have much more sediment. The river would be much more turbid.” A refugium of native fish, the Grand Canyon would suddenly be swamped with non-native fish, many of which were introduced into Lake Powell for sport fishing. “It just keeps getting more complicated,” Schmidt acknowledges. “It’s all a trade-off in this screwy manmade world.”

For now, Fill Mead First remains a pipe dream, one that’s getting a lot more attention as river levels continue to drop and global temperatures rise. The federal government will ultimately decide the Glen Canyon Dam’s future, but Eric Balken, for one, thinks a new regime is long overdue. Propping up Lake Powell is “kicking the can down the road,” he said. “But they are running out of road.”

stories.title: A New Dawn For Mathematical Progress
