stories.body:
Artificial intelligence is already a transformative chapter in the story of mathematics, but it won’t be the final one.

Atoosa Kasirzadeh is a philosopher and mathematician. She is a research scientist at DeepMind Institute and an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University. Her research is focused on the social and scientific implications of AI.

In the past few months, unreleased frontier AI systems have significantly disrupted a classic conception of mathematics. They successfully established a complete formalization of Andrew Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, found a solution to the Navier-Stokes problem and — just a few days ago — generated hundreds of manuscripts that each purport to prove an important mathematical problem. Most recently, on October 26, another of the Clay Millennium Prize problems was felled by an AI system.

Mathematicians reacted with a volatile mixture of optimism, anxiety and deep disorientation. In July, for example, Kirwin Hampshire, a Ph.D. student in mathematics, published an essay he titled “The Dark Night of Mathematics” in which he voiced the fear that human mathematicians might soon become obsolete next to AI systems with far greater speed and memory. “I am suffering a profound spiritual crisis due to these developments,” he wrote. “I have been screaming internally for days. It feels as though I am living inside of a nightmare.” For Hampshire, the very act of doing mathematics — the human struggle, the human aesthetic judgment, the human feeling and value of finding, understanding and sharing a new proof — could become a quaint artisanal craft, with human mathematicians no longer needed to push the frontier of mathematics.

Some mathematicians have realized that they must radically rethink their professional role and identity in light of this new technological reality. I was recently at an AI conference where a Fields Medal winner gave a talk on the frontier capabilities of AI systems for math problems. They closed their talk by saying: “We need to develop new theories of care and love.” This call was quite telling: a world-class mathematical theorist asking for theories of a very different kind. The mathematician, it seems, might become a philosopher of care and love. In a short essay, Logan Graves, a mathematical philosopher, went further , suggesting that “the era of human mathematicians is ending, if not ended ”; human mathematicians should find a new purpose in life, he wrote, and “the future of the human mathematical community, and eventually all scientific communities, is the practice of priests, then that of monks. Not researchers.”

Terence Tao, a prominent Fields Medal winner and mathematics professor, acknowledged the deep complexity of this historical moment. Adopting a cautiously optimistic stance, he forecast that the mathematical “community will emerge stronger and more resilient than before.” Daniel Litt, a professor of mathematics at the University of Toronto, offered a set of core problems that should be solved for building the future of mathematics in an intriguing essay called “The End of Mathematics.” Litt wrote: “I’m broadly optimistic that mathematics will survive and flourish,” but that requires the mathematical community to address complex (not merely formal) questions such as redesigning institutions that incentivize high-quality scientific research and reorienting human capital.

Each of these reactions is entirely understandable; each represents a deeply respectable and admirable attempt to face and process a disruption to established ways of doing, being or becoming — of doing a certain type of mathematics and of being or becoming a particular type of mathematician.

Because these reactions respond to different dimensions of a complex concern, it is helpful to distinguish between four central questions that urgently need answers. First: What is mathematical progress, and how is mathematics actually advanced? Second: How is the epistemic and creative agency of practicing mathematicians being disrupted? Third: How should we educate future human mathematicians and sustain human mathematical capacities? And fourth: How should incentives, research and structures for reward and credit be reorganized?

I start by distinguishing between two models of mathematical progress. I call them the checklist model and the generative encounter model . In the checklist model, mathematical progress is primarily about incremental advancement in proving what humans, at a rather recent point in our history, have designated a checklist of “major mathematical problems.” The generative encounter model, on the other hand, conceptualizes mathematical progress as inherently open-ended and unfinished, and its development, for the time being, is subject to negotiation with definitions of human purpose, desire and experience.

“Mathematics is one of the greatest things humans have built. Like all our built things, it keeps changing as we change — and our understanding of it keeps changing too.”

The Checklist Model

Under the checklist model, mathematical progress consists of resolving well-defined, complex problems that are specified in advance. These include competition problems designed to measure the frontier of human mathematical capabilities such as those of the International Mathematical Olympiad, famous conjectures such as Fermat’s Last Theorem (or last conjecture), formalization benchmarks such as Freek Wiedijk’s list of 100 formalization challenges and prize problems such as Clay’s Millennium problems. Each of these can be considered an item on a checklist. Mathematical progress proceeds at rate at which the boxes get ticked, and reward and credit attribution goes to whoever ticks them first. This model of mathematical progress is attractive because it is neat and it makes progress easily measurable. That is why it underpins both the prestige economy of mathematics (Olympiad medals, the Fields Medal, the Millennium Prizes) and the benchmark culture of AI.

AI systems have been rapidly excelling at solving a checklist of major mathematical problems. Some mathematicians like Tao refer to a new age of “proof post-scarcity” in which checklists of mathematical conjectures, including ones to be added in the future, are quickly proved or disproved one after the other by increasingly powerful AI systems.

A subset of the mathematical community has long organized its conception of progress around this model and the straightforward systems for reward and credit that it produces. Whoever solves a major problem from a canonical checklist earns the credit, and that cements their status as a genius (often a lone genius, which is important). Entire research and academic institutions grew up around this incentive structure, and generations of students were taught that (one of) their highest aspirations should be to solve (at least) one of these problems. Now that AI systems can solve these problems, the norm that reserved such achievements exclusively for humans, and rewarded humans for them, no longer carries the social weight it once did. This means that, as Cornell mathematics professor Steven Strogatz said in a recent interview , the age of lone human mathematical heroes is over.

But the end of the lone human hero is not the end of human mathematicians.

AI is showing us that the incentives around the checklist model are not sustainable anymore. While loss and grief are valid responses to this new reality, remaining stuck there leaves the community unable to respond to radically transformative changes. We should look at this historical moment as an opportunity to redesign the structures that motivate and reward mathematical work, and we should do it soon.

“AI brings us back to an old philosophical question: Where does mathematics come from?”

The checklist model rests on a remarkably narrow conception of mathematical inquiry. Even before AI systems started solving problems, the model didn’t seem to directly serve real-world problems. Many mathematicians have long worked in “exploratory mode,” disregarding questions about whether their lines of inquiry had any practical usefulness. G.H. Hardy, an English mathematician who died in 1947, is famous for writing “I have never done anything ‘useful.’ No discovery of mine has made, or is likely to make, directly or indirectly, for good or ill, the least difference to the amenity of the world.”

If mathematical progress is bound to the values of human mathematicians who can decide what to formalize, determine which problems truly matter, co-create with software and artificial agents and invent or discover novel domains of inquiry, then AI does not signal an end for the field. Instead, it opens a vast, unprecedented space of possibility.

The checklist model of mathematical progress is not representative of the actual progress in “mathematics” when we look at the history of the field. Under its narrow view, the pessimism of some mathematicians ( We are becoming obsolete ; There is no need for future humans to do mathematics ; No valuable rewards for doing mathematics remain for humans now ) offers no guidance about what mathematicians should do next.

Under a different model of mathematical progress, which I call the generative encounter model, proving major problems is just one piece of “doing mathematics” or “being a mathematician.” Here, AI’s impact on the mathematical community, generational education and institutional design is much more open to constructive and creative adjustment.

The Generative Encounter Model

In 1939, George Dantzig arrived late to a statistics class during his doctoral studies at Berkeley and found two problems written on the blackboard. He thought they were homework assignments from the professor, Jerzy Neyman, so he solved them and handed in his work. “About six weeks later,” according to his own account, Dantzig and his wife “were awakened by someone banging on our front door. It was Neyman. He rushed in with papers in hand, all excited.” The problems weren’t homework, it turned out, but rather famous unsolved problems, and Neyman wanted to rush to publish Dantzig’s work.

After Berkeley, Dantzig became an adviser to the U.S. Air Force Comptroller. He was tasked with finding a way to mechanize the planning and budgeting of the military’s staggering logistical operations. The reality he faced was one of worldly complexity. Thousands of human clerks were tasked with drafting and creating supply-chain and personnel schedules entirely by hand, using heuristic trial-and-error.

There were no preexisting mathematical problems for Dantzig to solve here. He faced the chaotic physical reality and had to figure out how to translate it into a useful mathematical abstraction. This is an example of an “encounter” in the generative encounter model: a social and practical problem with apparently little to do with “just proving” mathematics.

As Dantzig himself later recounted in an interview, the military used the word “program” — not computer code but rather a plan or a schedule. Dantzig’s goal, therefore, became simply to more rapidly develop a program for time-staged deployment, training and logistics. He was not trying to prove a theorem or conjecture; he was not hired for that, nor did he expect an award for developing such a thing. He was trying to fix an administrative bottleneck.

To do so, he invented (or discovered, if you like) a class of problems that needed solving. He did this by structuring and interpreting the situation into an elegant formulation composed of two distinct parts: a linear objective to be achieved (maximize efficiency or minimize cost, for example) and a set of constraints expressed as a system of linear inequalities (a certain number of planes, pilots, gallons of fuel, etc.). He called this mathematical package a “linear programming problem.” The word “programming” he borrowed directly from the military’s administrative vocabulary.

By mathematically separating the physical constraints from the ultimate goal and approximating both with linear relationships, Dantzig mapped a messy real-world problem onto a clean, high-dimensional geometric object: a convex polyhedron. This abstraction transformed a question of scheduling human action and materials into a question of geometry, and in doing so, made it a part of an open-ended conception of mathematics .

Dantzig had taste. He made a crucial recognition: As a matter of mathematical necessity, the optimal solution to a programming problem would lie on one of the vertices of a polyhedron. The search for the “best” mathematical solution or the best “schedule” thus became a search for the “highest” corner of a geometric object. Dantzig then developed the now-famous simplex algorithm to systematically search for that optimal vertex by efficiently moving along the edges of the polyhedron until reaching the peak.

Before Dantzig, there was no mathematical community of “linear programmers” listing out problems in their field and seeking to solve them. He formed a community, one that grew to include operations researchers, mathematical economists and industrial engineers as additional sub-branches of the field were developed. This group defined itself by a shared interest in a set of problems that had not existed a decade earlier.

Linear programming works for continuous resources like gallons of fuel, but what if a problem demands whole units? You cannot fly half an airplane or assign a third of a pilot to a mission. That physical constraint, a new encounter, forced the invention of a branch of operations research known as integer programming . This, in turn, opened a vast new frontier of mathematics, generating entirely new branches of mathematics, theoretical models and novel algorithms, which themselves collided with new problems and produced yet more fields of inquiry .

“A revolution in automated proof discovery, on its own, guarantees nothing definite about the future of mathematics, which remains an open-ended domain of inquiry.”

Before the MIT mathematician Norbert Wiener created the field we now call cybernetics , which later formed the backbone of modern artificial intelligence, he was confronted with a wartime problem similar in some ways to the one that faced Dantzig: how to shoot a plane out of the sky using an antiaircraft gun on the ground when the enemy pilot was taking evasive action. Aiming at the plane guaranteed a miss, so where do you aim? As Wiener later put it, “It is exceedingly important to shoot the missile, not at the target, but in such a way that missile and target may come together in space at some time in the future. We must hence find some method of predicting the future position of the plane.” This problem was not on any checklist of mathematical problems. It had to be encountered.

Wiener’s move was to reframe the problem. He stopped treating a pilot as a strategic adversary to be outguessed and instead considered him a component in a system to be characterized. He saw that the pilot’s evasive maneuvers were not purely random; they were responses to the gunner’s actions and corrections against the aircraft’s physical lags. In this view, the gunner, the antiaircraft gun, the shell, the pilot and the aircraft all formed a single system with different feedback loops between them. To this loop Wiener added what he called a predictor.

In his 1948 book “ Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine ,” Wiener described the task as designing a predictor whose characteristics “depend[ed] on a long-time acquaintance with the statistics of the ensemble of time series which we desire to predict.” In this sentence, the significance of real-world encounters for mathematical progress becomes quite obvious. The physical problem of gunnery was converted into a statistical problem about time. This conversion created a cluster of new mathematical problems: What is the optimal filter to separate a signal from noise? How can one best predict the future course of a random process from its past? What, formally, does it even mean for a system to be goal-directed?

The answers gave birth to the theory of statistical filtering and prediction and ultimately the feedback formalism that organized the new mathematics and science of cybernetics. Wiener created a new branch of mathematics for describing, explaining, understanding and predicting control and communication in both machines and living organisms. It generated a new community, a new field, which brought different epistemic stances together to better understand the world. The now-famous Macy Conferences in the late 1940s and early 1950s brought together biologists, psychiatrists, anthropologists and engineers around a set of problems that previously had no disciplinary home. Cybernetics, as a new branch of mathematics, created a new home for such inquiries. Read Noema in print.

Most telling of all, the original purpose that sparked the work was soon superseded. Wiener’s antiaircraft predictor was not widely deployed; a simpler design from Bell Labs won the military contract. Had it been a problem on a checklist, Wiener’s project might be seen as a failure, seeing as how it was an inferior solution to another. But the mathematics it created survived and went on to reshape our understanding of many systems, from factory automation to human and artificial neural systems.

There Is No Distinction Between Pure And Applied Mathematics. There Is Only Mathematics.

During my doctoral studies in mathematics (in the field of “operations research”), I attended a national conference for mathematical graduate students in Canada. The atmosphere was charged with a peculiar intellectual stratification between “pure” (or “real”) mathematics and “applied” mathematics.

When some of my peers, who were working on classical analytic number theory and variations of the Riemann hypothesis, learned that others of us were researching mathematical and computational approaches for large-scale decision problems, their response was immediate and dismissive: What you do is not real mathematics. To them, real mathematical inquiry belonged exclusively to the solitary pursuit of proving major theorems within self-contained axiomatic systems. Not considered real mathematics were efforts to develop and formulate algorithms to solve large-scale decision problems, optimize resource distribution, translate frictions and decision problems into mathematical structures, and perhaps find new theories of decision-making in real-world encounters.

The culture of mathematicians has for generations harbored a hidden hierarchy between these two communities of mathematicians: Generating abstract proofs supposedly constituted “real” mathematics whereas dealing with the messy, empirical world was dismissed as an inferior craft. Historically, this divide served a practical purpose: It functioned as a tool for creating an epistemic division of labor, organizing mathematical activity and giving rise to separate institutions, journals and reward structures for tackling a variety of different cognitive engagements with mathematical problems.

By placing the generation of proofs for very complex problems at the apex of this hierarchy, the pure-applied dichotomy, perhaps unintentionally, popularized the idea that pure mathematics is (real) mathematics. In doing so, it enshrined the checklist model of mathematical progress, leading many to mistake measuring a peculiar type of epistemic activity for the entirety of mathematical progress. The conflation of the title mathematician with those who study only pure mathematics is a pervasive and uncritical cultural prejudice. It is one that relegates researchers who grapple with physical and systemic realities to second-class status. I think AI has forced us to correct that prejudice, and I do not think we can ignore it.

“A true golden age of mathematics, rooted in human purpose and new visions of education and collective reward, may have just begun.”

Dantzig too faced gatekeeping by pure mathematicians, whose insistence that their work was the only “real” mathematics generated a highly exclusionary perception of the discipline. When asked whether he thought of himself as an operations researcher or a mathematician, Dantzig answered: “I consider myself a mathematician. I don’t differentiate between pure mathematics and applied mathematics. I know other people will tell you there is a difference, but there isn’t.”

When the interviewer noted that pure mathematicians often describe operations researchers as “second-rate mathematicians playing with toy problems,” Dantzig’s response was characteristically blunt: “Mathematicians are snobs.”

“Present company excepted,” the interviewer responded. “Pure math involves clean problems, but real-world problems are messy.”

“Real-world problems are all dirty, that’s correct,” Dantzig said. “Any model of them is an approximation of reality; it’s not reality.”

Dantzig’s experience in the development of linear programming led him to become a strong advocate of encountered problems as the inspiration for interesting and challenging mathematical work. Speaking to Donald Albers in 1984, he said:

Just because my mathematics has its origin in a real problem doesn’t make it less interesting to me—just the other way around, I find it makes the puzzle I am working on all the more exciting. I get satisfaction out of knowing that I’m working on a relevant problem. I find that just as much mathematical ingenuity has to go into solving problems from a newly developing area as from some old so-called pure math area.

Operations research, Dantzig went on, is the “science of decision-making”: the art of “abstracting a problem and putting it into mathematical form.” For him, mathematical practice spans a continuous spectrum from the abstract theorist seeking formal solutions down to the practitioner needing an actionable answer to a concrete crisis. To chop this continuum in half and declare one end “noble” and the other “second-class” misses the entire dynamic essence of mathematical inquiry.

The “crisis” of AI’s ability to rapidly solve complex problems, and mathematicians’ responsibility for building infrastructure for mathematical inquiry in the near future, can be seen in a new light. A messy encounter with the world, after all, can be the birthplace of the purest mathematics, and pure mathematics can find its way back to the world.

Powerful Systems, Open Futures

We must approach this historical moment with the utmost care. The main challenge is not only to mourn a loss. It is, more importantly, to build a better future. The development and deployment of AI is forcing us to redraw the maps of human motivation, reward and research prestige in mathematics. Redrawing those maps does not have to erase human agency — but it can if approached clumsily.

If we restructure how we assign credit, set research priorities and reward work — moving away from proof discovery alone — we can cultivate “Dantzig-style” mathematical thinkers. These are people who use AI to free their creative faculties and push into deeper, more interesting or more urgent territory.

This moment has opened a vast space of possibilities. New incentives can be designed around problems that genuinely matter for better human life, for individual and social health, for planetary flourishing. And we are not short of those problems.

Perhaps the mathematical community and its future generations can move from “ Who proved it?” to “ Who decided this was worth proving, why, and how did we make sure it was right?” Large collaborations already exist in mathematics: the Polymath projects, the Lean community’s Mathlib, the long effort to formalize Fermat’s Last Theorem. Mathematicians can coordinate around shared goals that matter for their community, but also for the world.

They now need to scale coordination capabilities. But how?

I think the mathematical community must embrace the generative encounter model of mathematical progress. This requires that we treat the integration of AI in mathematics as a rich, independent subject of foundational analysis. Far from signaling the end of mathematics, this opens room for examining a vast frontier of urgent, encountered mathematical problems that require deep work, often in collaboration with other disciplines. Here are four critical clusters of mathematical problems where this work is urgently needed:

Provably safe cyber infrastructure . Our global digital systems remain profoundly fragile. Human mathematicians, using AI as a high-throughput collaborative partner, can work to find the flaws and rebuild our cyber foundations from first principles, establishing provably secure and mathematically verified computing environments.

The epistemic mechanics of deep learning . Our mathematical grasp of how neural networks learn, generalize and represent high-dimensional data is still in its infancy. Several concerns about advanced AI causing catastrophic harm originate directly from this gap in understanding. Despite significant advances, developing a rigorous “mathematical science of deep learning” remains a fundamental challenge, and solving it is a precondition for building truly trustworthy systems.

The mathematics of multi-agent control . The dynamic alignment or misalignment of interacting, agentic AI systems remains poorly understood . We need to draw on mathematical disciplines such as mathematical security, safety engineering, robust mechanism design and game theory to analyze how individually optimized agents behave when they coordinate, compete or collide.

The epistemology of machine-generated proofs . What should we do with AI-generated “proofs” that are too long, too complex, or too alien for human minds to understand or verify ? Rather than rejecting them because they are unintelligible, we must develop new mathematical techniques for explanation, logical translation and interactive verification that make them understandable. We shouldn’t rush to rely on such proofs, but these techniques can give us reliable paths for turning raw automated output into genuine human understanding.

None of these problems appear on a checklist of mathematical problems. None of them will be easily “solved” by a single human mathematician. Each needs teams of humans equipped with technological tools to decide what and how to formalize and interpret mathematical problems that matter — and how to build institutions to apply the offered solutions.

The world around us is human-made: the buildings, the networks, the institutions, the AI models themselves. Mathematics is one of the greatest things humans have built. Like all our built things, it keeps changing as we change — and our understanding of it keeps changing too.

This brings us back to an old philosophical question: Where does mathematics come from? The cognitive scientists George Lakoff and Rafael Núñez gave one answer in their book “ Where Mathematics Comes From ”: embodied human cognition. Platonists give another: Mathematics is discovered, not made. Its objects exist independently of humans, and mathematicians are explorers of a terrain that has been there all along and will still be there in the absence of any human. Formalists give a third response: Mathematics is a game of symbols and rules, and it is “true” only in the sense that a legal chess move is correct. I won’t settle the debate here. But every answer locates at least part of the origin of mathematics in an encounter: between minds and the world, between us and Plato’s heaven, or between human communities and the questions they find worth asking and answering. AI systems have now become a serious participant in that encounter.

A revolution in automated proof discovery, on its own, guarantees nothing definite about the future of mathematics, which remains an open-ended domain of inquiry. That future will be shaped not only by AIs but also by the preconditions that make doing mathematics possible, or impossible: the purposes, infrastructure and institutions we build around the questions we find worth asking and answering. These include how to verify results, how to assign credit, how to train students, how to value human cognition and agency, how to support those harmed by this transition and give them new systems of recognition to rely on, how to advance human and planetary flourishing, how to make tools and infrastructure broadly accessible and who sits at the table when these questions are answered.

Answering these questions requires science and mathematics as necessary elements of the sociotechnical foundation for a better future. And that we do not yet have.

“New incentives can be designed around problems that genuinely matter for better human life, for individual and social health, for planetary flourishing. And we are not short of those problems.”

Viewed from the generative encounter model of mathematical progress, a true golden age of mathematics, rooted in human purpose and new visions of education and collective reward, may have just begun.

Suppose this situation and these questions are only temporary. What about later? What if we eventually build artificial superintelligence — systems that don’t just prove theorems but pose questions, judge which ones matter, design curricula and decide how rewards are distributed? Systems that automate the whole process of generative encounters?

The deepest version of the worry some “pure” mathematicians are articulating is not whether AI can automate mathematical proofs. It is whether AI eventually automates human purpose itself. But let’s not forget how we arrived here.

Our current moment is, among other things, a long-term consequence of the dream of formalizing mathematics, from the well-posed formulas of mathematical logic that gave rise to software engineering to the contemporary drive in the Lean community to formalize mathematics in machine-readable form so that machines might verify and, one day, prove or solve problems. In some sense, where we are today is partly the realization of a long dream held by a portion of the mathematical community. But living in a realized dream requires us to think carefully not just about the dream itself, but about its consequences. Purpose matters.

Whether the day ever comes when human purpose is fully automated none of us can know. But what is clear is that the future is shaped by what we dream and build today, and we owe it to ourselves, our children and future generations to dream and build it with care. In the end, the transition to the future is not separate from the future. And the transition is where the future is actually lived, dreamed and made.

Author’s note: Thanks to Jim Brown, Marcus Hutter and Shane Legg for comments on this essay.

stories.body:
Shabana Mahmood has backed down on two elements

Published 2 November 2026

Today's announcement has long been viewed in government as a potential political banana skin.

When the home secretary announced her first version of changes to the settlement system last year, many Labour MPs, including the housing secretary Angela Rayner, voiced their concerns about the plans.

But there was a feeling that Sir Keir Starmer's government was determined to plough on regardless. Shabana Mahmood herself repeatedly expressed how important she believed the reforms were.

But the change of prime minister over the summer gave renewed hope to those unhappy Labour MPs that they could force the Home Office into two changes.

Firstly, social care workers – under the original plans many social care workers would have had to wait 15 years before becoming eligible for settlement.

Secondly, the retrospective nature of the plans – some MPs were uncomfortable at the idea of someone coming to the UK and expecting to be eligible for settlement after five years, but then having to wait longer.

Angela Rayner described that as "un-British" and said the government shouldn't be shifting "the goalposts".

She returned to the cabinet under Andy Burnham as housing secretary and chose to repeat those criticisms in an interview during the Labour Party conference in September.

That was seen as evidence that a debate inside the top levels of government about whether to water down the plans was well and truly rumbling on.

For all the Labour MPs who wanted a change, there were others, particularly those in Brexit-supporting areas, who wanted the home secretary to stick the course.

Some inside government felt nervous about providing what they saw as catnip to Reform and the Conservatives.

All of that added up to one of the more difficult decisions that has had to be taken since Burnham walked through the doors of Number 10.

In the end ministers chose to water down the proposals for care workers – those who arrived before May 2025 and earn at least £25,000 a year will qualify for settlement in five years.

But the retrospective nature of the plans, the thing Rayner described as shifting "the goalposts", hasn't changed.

Despite that, the majority of Labour MPs pulled their punches when Mahmood made a statement in the House of Commons earlier .

Perhaps the strongest pushback came from Rachael Maskell, who is no fan of the retrospective element - but others on the left of the party, including John McDonnell and Diane Abbott, were critical without being scathing.

Mahmood scraps settlement plans for migrant care workers Published 7 hours ago

What are the planned changes to immigration rules? Published 17 hours ago

Outside the Commons chamber, the mood among Labour folk was pretty similar to what was said from the green benches.

One would-be critic said that while they personally still had concerns about the plans announced today, they believed the Home Secretary had successfully taken the political sting out of the situation for now.

They said the campaign by MPs and unions had led to a "big win" on settlement for social care workers, but said they were still expecting to hear from constituents negatively affected by the new rules.

One Number 10 source praised Mahmood's "take no prisoners" performance in the chamber, argued she had "found the right balance" and said the announcement had gone down as well as could be expected with Labour colleagues.

Of course, the home secretary will still need to deal with criticism from other parties.

Her opposite number for the Conservatives, Chris Philp, accused Mahmood of a significant U-turn.

Philp highlighted a claim she had previously made – that allowing care workers to reach settlement more quickly could cost the UK £10bn.

The social care workers plans announced today will see around 500,000 people have their path to settlement delayed , that number would have been around 800,000 under the original plans last year.

In an interview with the BBC, Mahmood wouldn't say what sort of financial burden her watering down would result in.

She also refused to confirm whether Burnham had directly asked her to water down the plans.

They are tricky questions that she will have to navigate over the coming weeks.

But the general view within government is that this is one political hurdle that has been successfully jumped.

stories.title: PM plans debt reset for Commonwealth nations as slavery apology talks begin

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
King Charles III with Prime Minister Andy Burnham at a Commonwealth Business Forum in Antigua

Published 3 November 2026, 00:26 GMT

The prime minister will join the King at the formal opening of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua later - and begin talks with fellow leaders about the UK issuing a formal apology for the slave trade in the next year.

As part of the discussions, Downing Street said Andy Burnham would set out his plans for what it is calling a "debt reset" to support Commonwealth countries having to deal with the growing costs of paying interest on their debts.

The issue of reparations, compensation to those who were the victims of slavery, has dominated debate in the build up to this summit, in which representatives from 56 Commonwealth countries are meeting.

"Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting," the prime minister said, in a tacit acknowledgement that the last Commonwealth gathering, on the Pacific island of Samoa two years ago, did not go well from a UK perspective.

The previous Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer had said prior to the meeting that reparations were not on the agenda , but other leaders insisted they should be.

This time, the new prime minister has sought to get ahead of the debate, and appeared to directly address the anger of some Commonwealth leaders after the last summit.

"For years, those members of the Commonwealth affected by the slave trade have asked for an honest conversation about the legacies of slavery , external . By sticking our heads in the sand, we have damaged the ability of the Commonwealth to function," Burnham argued in an article in the Guardian.

Burnham alongside the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and the former Prime Minister Gordon Brown, are beginning conversations which, they hope, will help detoxify the debate about reparations.

They do so while insisting the UK will not pay them, but is likely to formally apologise for the slave trade for the first time next year, when the UK holds the rotating presidency of the G20 group of countries.

"A formal apology," Miliband said in a social media video , external , is something "the British government are open to".

He said this would be a "significant step" but added that "we don't believe financial reparations are the right or feasible answer to transatlantic slavery. We don't think the right response is to ask British taxpayers today to make financial payments for these historic acts."

King's role is not policy making, says Palace in slavery apology row Published 13 hours ago

No10 defends flight to Manchester to collect Andy Burnham Published 19 hours ago

King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology Published 1 day ago

The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has urged the prime minister not to issue an apology for slavery, saying it would give countries a reason to ask the UK for reparations.

She said: "I don't think we should be giving any money to compensate people for the slave trade, and I don't think that Andy Burnham needs to be apologising because it is a lever to wedge open the door to ask for cash."

But British officials are hopeful, even confident, that the prime minister and foreign secretary's approach will create space in the next two days for a wider conversation with fellow Commonwealth countries.

No 10 said the UK would lead two new task forces - one focused on critical mineral assets and vulnerabilities in supply chains across the group and the other aimed at boosting trade and investment more widely.

Both will be set up by the end of the year and report back at the next leaders' summit, officials said.

British diplomats view the Commonwealth as a useful forum for conversations with developing countries, and, crucially, one that does not involve China, America or Russia.

stories.title: What are the planned changes to immigration rules?
stories.summary: The home secretary sets out plans to change requirements for permanent settlement in the UK.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood set out the plans in the House of Commons

Published 2 November 2026

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has set out plans to overhaul immigration rules.

Proposals to change the requirements to qualify for permanent settlement in the UK were first outlined in detail in November 2025, when Mahmood was home secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government.

Following a consultation , external , Mahmood has now announced her final decision on what changes should be taken forward.

Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes Published 2 hours ago

Mahmood scraps settlement plans for migrant care workers Published 7 hours ago

What is settlement and indefinite leave to remain?

Indefinite leave to remain (ILR) – also known as settlement – gives someone the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like.

Under the current system, people with ILR can also apply for benefits if they are eligible.

People who have lived in the UK for 12 months after being given ILR can apply for British citizenship, if they also meet other requirements , external .

How will the new rules affect migrants?

Under the government's plans, the standard length of time migrants will have to live in the UK to qualify for permanent settlement will double from five to 10 years.

Under this 10-year pathway, applicants must have earned at least £12,571 for five of the seven years immediately before being granted settlement.

However, there will be a shorter qualifying period of five years for certain groups, including:

People who earned at least £50,271 for three of five years immediately before applying for settlement

Care workers who earned at least £25,000 a year while meeting their visa conditions and arrived in the UK before May 2025

"Skilled" public service workers, such as doctors, nurses and teachers

Other health and education public service workers who fall below this skill level, for example nursing auxiliaries and teaching assistants, if they arrived in the UK before May 2025

People from Hong Kong who hold British National (Overseas) status

People earning over £125,141 a year, as well as "highly skilled" migrants such as those on Global Talent or Innovator Founder visas, will qualify after three years.

Migrants who have claimed certain benefits or breached immigration rules will only be able to settle after at least 20 years.

To qualify for settlement, migrants will also have to meet other conditions including:

Have no criminal record

Speak English to a high standard

Owe no debt to the taxpayer

Earn at least £12,571 a year for at least three years, aligned with the threshold for paying income tax

Some care workers will be able to qualify for settlement after five years

What about refugees?

There will be a different set of rules for refugees – people who have been granted asylum in the UK because they are unable to return to their own country as they fear persecution.

Refugees who arrived in the UK through an official government scheme will qualify for settlement after five years.

However, other refugees will need to wait 10 years and either work or study.

Those who do not work or study will need to wait 20 years.

Refugees who arrived in the UK by small boat or another illegal route will have to wait 20 years if they work or study, and 30 years if they don't.

Will migrants already in the UK be affected?

The changes will apply to migrants who are already in the UK but not those who have already been granted settlement.

What about family members?

A partner who arrives with someone who then applies for ILR will be able to settle at the same time, as long as they meet the relevant requirements.

However, a partner who joins later will need to complete the same qualifying residence period before they are eligible for settlement.

Eligible couples will be able to combine their earnings to meet the minimum income requirement.

The household income threshold will be £25,142 – twice the individual minimum income requirement.

Children under 18 will continue to be able to settle with their parents.

They will be exempt from the income, government debt, English language and Life in the UK test requirements, but will remain subject to the relevant suitability and criminality requirements.

Young adults aged 18 to 24, who remain dependant on their family, will also continue to be able to settle alongside them.

They will be expected to meet all the adult mandatory requirements but not the individual income requirement.

Someone who is aged 25 or over when their family becomes eligible for settlement will be expected to qualify independently.

Eligible partners, parents and children of British citizens will continue to qualify for settlement after five years.

stories.title: Reform council leader quits after staff comments leaked
stories.summary: Dan Harrison was recorded as saying 76 council solicitors he branded "incompetent" would be made redundant.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Dan Harrison previously said his leaked remarks had been taken out of context

Published 2 November 2026

The Reform UK leader of Leicestershire County Council has announced he is standing down after comments he made about staff redundancies were leaked online.

Dan Harrison announced on Monday that he would be stepping down from the role he has held since May 2025.

He said he had made the decision after taking advice from senior Reform colleagues, and added deputy council leader Kevin Crook had taken over as acting leader.

It comes after Harrison had apologised after being recorded saying 76 council solicitors would be made redundant, branding them "incompetent", before saying "what I want to look at now is the women", in remarks which were then released on social media.

In a statement, Harrison said it had been the "honour of his life" to lead the county council's first Reform administration.

Harrison has said he will remain as a councillor, representing the Ashby-de-la-Zouch division.

The Conservative opposition at County Hall had called for Harrison to resign after his comments about staff were leaked.

In the recording, Harrison said: "There's 76 solicitors will be made redundant.

"We'll buy in the service, because [they are] incompetent. They're not doing a good job.

"What I want to look at now is the women so it is ongoing, I would like it to be at great pace but I can tell you now if we suddenly drove massive redundancies the liberals would walk away."

Conservative group leader Deborah Taylor had called for an emergency vote to try to oust Harrison

Earlier on Monday, Harrison had told the BBC he would not be stepping down - but he later said he made his decision after talking to Crook and group whip Andrew Hamilton-Gray.

He had apologised over the remarks, which were made on Tuesday during a Reform party meeting.

Despite his apology, Harrison had insisted his remarks had been taken out of context.

Harrison said: "I would like to apologise unreservedly to the staff and officers of the county council for any hurt, distress or offence caused by the publication of these comments, which were made during a heated meeting with the expectation of privacy and confidentiality.

"However, I would like to stress that these discussions were just that, and I have not given any instruction or direction to officers in these matters and that there has not been any discussion nor agreement on these issues with officers."

He added: "I unequivocally reject any suggestion that staffing decisions are being taken based on gender.

"The comments made in that meeting were taken completely out of context."

Position 'untenable'

Before Harrison's resignation, the council's 15 Tory councillors had called for an emergency vote to try to remove him from the leader's role.

Group leader of the Conservative group, Deborah Taylor, said: "That was not a decision we took lightly.

"The serious concerns raised over recent days, particularly around the treatment of council employees and the comments contained in leaked recordings, left us feeling that his position had become untenable.

"His resignation brings an end to his leadership, but it does not mean those concerns should simply be forgotten.

"There are still questions that deserve answers, and it is important that the council learns from what has happened."

The Reform group remains the largest party on the authority, and runs it as a minority administration.

In a statement, Jeevun Sandher and Amanda Hack - Labour MPs for Loughborough and North West Leicestershire respectively - said: "Since taking office in 2025, the Reform UK administration has become increasingly embroiled in controversy and scandal, rather than focusing on delivering for the residents of Leicestershire.

"This is far from an isolated incident. Just last week, councillor [Joseph] Boam was found to have breached the council's own code of conduct through his actions against the former monitoring officer, while other Reform councillors have also been forced to apologise to residents over their behaviour. All of this in less than two years.

"Leicestershire residents deserve better."

stories.title: No10 defends flight to Manchester to collect Andy Burnham
stories.summary: The trip sparked a backlash with some questioning the value for money, but No 10 says security, cost and "operational requirements" were all factored in.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Andy Burnham and his wife took the plane to the United Nations in the US in September

Published 2 November 2026

Downing Street has defended sending the official UK government plane to Manchester to pick up Andy Burnham, rather than the prime minister travelling to London in advance of the flight.

The Airbus A321neo departed London Stansted Airport for Saint John's, the capital of Antigua and Barbuda, at about 06:00 on Monday without the prime minister on board.

Half an hour later it landed in Manchester to collect Burnham, before taking off again to cross the Atlantic for the Commonwealth heads of government summit (Chogm).

The trip sparked a backlash on social media with some questioning the value for money, but Number 10 said security, cost and "operational requirements" were all factored in.

The official UK government plane , carrying the registration G-GBNI, is often used by British prime ministers and royals for overseas trips.

Flight tracking data shows the jet made a 35 minute flight on Monday morning to Manchester, where it spent an hour and a half on the tarmac, before taking off at 08:00 to head to St John's.

In response, Tory MP and shadow cabinet minister Neil O'Brien accused Labour of managing to "waste taxpayers' money and jet fuel so they can posture".

"You have to pay through the nose for energy and fuel to pursue their Net Zero obsession... But when it's them, the rules are different," he added.

Asked why Burnham had not travelled to London instead, his official spokesperson told reporters: "The prime minister's travel arrangements reflect where he was carrying out official government business at the end of last week.

"As you know, he spent the day in Scotland on Friday; returned to Manchester to work from Number 10 North on Friday evening."

The official UK Government plane is used for the PM and royals

Burnham will meet Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday, coming at the end of the King's Caribbean tour , with the prime minister saying he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery.

It is unclear how much the London to Manchester trip cost, or whether there is a precedent for it, as the Cabinet Office's transparency data for the plane only lists overseas trips.

None of Burnham's trips are listed yet, as the data is published quarterly.

The latest data for April to June 2026 shows then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer made four round trips on the jet, including a £121,000 trip to Armenia with 21 officials for the European Political Community Summit.

A trip from the UK to Paris in April cost £39,000.

The precise cost of each flight can depend on how many officials were with the prime minister, fuel costs and other factors such as landing fees.

It is also unclear whether transporting the prime minister, his security detail and officials by train or road transport from Manchester to Stansted would have been much cheaper.

A previous version of the UK government official plane, an RAF Voyager, was given a £900,000 repaint job in 2020 before being replaced with a different plane.

stories.title: Labour ends power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
stories.summary: Labour's ruling National Executive Committee sets out where it is cutting ties with the Greens.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Greens have been in direct coalition with Labour on a handful of councils, including Sheffield

Published 2 November 2026

The Labour Party has pulled out of power-sharing agreements with the Green Party in 11 local councils, after the national party adopted a policy defining Zionism as a form of racism.

Labour councillors will no longer be in coalition with the Greens in areas including Sheffield, Warwick and Lewes.

Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson said: "Labour has been clear from the start that the "Zionism is Racism" policy crosses a line and we cannot work with any party that supports it – at any level of government."

Green leader Zack Polanski said the move would "backfire" on Labour and accused the party of wanting to "interrupt your local services and impose genocide support from it's local councils".

In October, Green Party members backed a motion, entitled "Zionism is racism", which said Zionism was an ideology that supported an "ethnonationalist Jewish State in historic Palestine". Israel has denied committing genocide in Gaza.

The motion also backed a "single democratic Palestinian State", including in modern-day Israel.

Having been backed by party members, the motion became Green Party policy, but it has left senior figures bitterly divided . Jewish groups and opposition political parties have condemned it.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs in October that Labour would not partner with the Greens over the "antisemitic" policy.

Labour then issued an ultimatum from Labour's head office to Labour-Green councils, demanding that local Greens disown the motion passed by members at their national party conference.

Green groups were also asked to call on their party's national leadership to reconsider the policy.

Labour said there were local agreements in place in 18 authorities. Of those, Labour said 11 had not met the criteria it demanded.

The areas are:

Arun District Council

Derbyshire Dales District Council

Havant Borough Council

Lewes District Council (The Green Party announced last week it was "mutually" ending its alliance with Labour)

Runnymede Borough Council (Labour says local co-operation had already ceased)

Sheffield City Council

Stafford Borough Council

Warwick District Council

Wealden District Council

West Devon Borough Council

West Suffolk Council

Labour said its conditions had been met in Broadland, Monmouthshire, North Somerset, Rother, West Oxfordshire and West Sussex. The party said that Coventry City Council does not have a formal arrangement in place and that no such deal will be made in the future.

It will continue co-operating with the Greens in the West of England mayoralty, where the deputy mayor is a Green member.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said the motion was "imperfect" but has defended its central premise , arguing that Israel's actions towards the Palestinian people are "clearly underpinned by racist ideology".

The collapse of co-operation at the local level could impact hundreds of thousands of residents through budgets and policy decisions taking longer to get voted through.

Green and Labour councillors in the impacted areas will now have to seek alternative coalition partners or try to govern as a minority administration.

In a joint statement, the Green Party and the Local Government Association Green Group said it was "hugely disappointed" that Labour had forced local leaders into "jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents".

'At the end of the road'

One of the biggest councils to be affected is Sheffield, where 25 Labour councillors formed a power-sharing agreement with 20 Green councillors after the May 2026 elections for the Yorkshire city's 550,000 residents.

Responding to Labour's ultimatum, leader of the Sheffield Greens Angela Argenzio did not mention the motion in a letter but insisted local Green councillors "are not antisemitic".

Argenzio told local Labour representatives they were being "directed by your national party leader" rather than local concerns.

In a statement on Monday, the council's Labour leader Cllr Fran Belbin said her party would propose on Wednesday that it proceeds as a Labour minority administration.

"We now feel we are at the end of the road with the joint administration," she said.

"Our trust in Sheffield Greens is completely broken," she added, accusing them of a "refusal to stand up for Jewish citizens".

'Complete disaster'

Green Party co-deputy leader Rachel Millward, also the leader of Wealden Council, said: "It is ironic that a Labour prime minister who made a promise to solve problems, not score points, has now shown he is willing to disrupt well-run councils for fear of Green success."

She added: "It is utterly irresponsible to conflate criticism of the actions of the state of Israel with antisemitism. Many Jewish people strongly reject the illegal actions of the current Israeli government."

In Warwick, the local Green party said: "We refuse to condemn a democratically decided policy because of political intimidation."

It urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to "reflect his own words in his actions and allow local Labour groups to decide for themselves".

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Green group leader in Havant Netty Shepherd accused Labour of "performative politics" and said the end of their coalition would be a "complete disaster for residents".

"I am a local government councillor, I worry about people's bins, I worry about generating town centres - foreign policy is nothing to do with my remit," she added.

The Liberal Democrats are also in partnership with the Green Party in some local councils.

Last week, the party leader Sir Ed Davey ruled out entering into a national partnership with "any party that is committed to a dangerous and antisemitic policy like the Green Party's".

He added that he had asked those of his local leaders in coalition with the Greens to urge Green councillors to reject the motion and commit to campaigning for its reversal.

stories.title: MP Carla Lockhart quits DUP in Drumcree row
stories.summary: Lockhart had called for the DUP to remove First Minister Michelle O'Neill from office.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Carla Lockhart is the MP for Upper Bann, a seat she has held since 2019

Published 2 November 2026

Carla Lockhart has quit the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) in a row over its response to the Drumcree parading dispute.

The MP for Upper Bann had been calling for the party to withdraw Stormont's deputy first minister to force First Minister Michelle O'Neill from their joint office.

Lockhart said she was leaving the DUP on a "point of principle" and would continue in the House of Commons as an independent unionist.

The fall-out comes after unionist anger over Sinn Féin's involvement in protests on Garvaghy Road , which blocked a contentious Orange Order parade from passing along the mainly nationalist street in Portadown, County Armagh.

O'Neill and several other senior Sinn Féin figures have been interviewed by police investigating the demonstrations, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.

Last week the DUP, which shares power with Sinn Féin in Northern Ireland's devolved government, announced it would block official engagements involving O'Neill in response to the fall-out.

The Sinn Féin vice-president has defended her involvement in the protests, saying it was the "right thing to do".

DUP leader Gavin Robinson stopped short of Lockhart's call to force O'Neill from office.

In an open letter to colleagues last week, Lockhart said it was the "only one credible option" and any kind of "graduated response" would be "insulting to those who have trusted us".

In a statement posted on her Facebook page on Monday, the MP said: "My first responsibility remains to the people of Upper Bann.

"You placed your trust in me, and I will continue to work every bit as hard for you, your family and our community."

Orangemen made numerous attempts to begin their march from Drumcree church

Lockhart said it was a "sad day and a deeply personal decision" but her departure from the DUP was "on a point of principle".

"I cannot stand idly by whilst Sinn Féin wilfully ignores the rule of law and the promised profound consequences fail to materialise," she added.

Lockhart concluded that she would "look forward to working with all shades of unionism, elected or not, to advance the cause we love".

The DUP said they regret Lockhart's decision to resign from the party

In a statement, the DUP said: "We regret Carla Lockhart's decision to resign from the Democratic Unionist Party. We thank her for her service to the party and recognise her work on behalf of the people of Upper Bann.

"The only winner out of further divisions within unionism is Sinn Féin."

It added: "We share the anger felt across unionism at Michelle O'Neill's actions. Our disagreement is over the course of action that will secure accountability and best serve Northern Ireland."

First Minister Michelle O'Neill joined protesters on the Garvaghy Road

In a statement, Traditional Unionist Voice leader Jim Allister congratulated Lockhart on her decision.

"Having myself resigned from the DUP almost 20 years ago, I know this was not an easy decision. But for honest politicians principle matters more than position.

"The DUP's preference for 'O'Neill Must Stay' caused them to choose Michelle O'Neill over Carla Lockhart. Little wonder their electoral base is deserting them."

Allister added that he looks forward "to working closely with Carla" and said it is "a hopeful day for unionism".

Analysis: Lockhart has been on a collision course for weeks

BBC News NI political editor Enda McClafferty

Cutting links with a party she first joined as a teenager was a big call for Carla Lockhart.

Her family ties to the DUP run deep prompting one colleague to say, "Carla bleeds the DUP".

But not anymore.

She has been on a collision course with the DUP leadership for weeks and now the "profound consequences" are being felt by the party.

Though she had some support within the DUP, she became a lone voice in her battle with the leadership.

She had the backing of Portadown Orangemen and many unionists, but Gavin Robinson crucially had the full support of the DUP officer and assembly teams.

He was able to face down the demands from his Upper Bann MP safe in the knowledge he had the numbers on his side.

Collapsing the executive without a budget agreed and running the risk of his party being blamed for a nurse's pay dispute strike was not a gamble he was willing to take.

But it has come at a cost for Robinson as he has now lost an MP from the DUP benches leaving just four for a party which once boasted ten members of parliament.

It has been a bruising time and one he needs to recover from quickly with just seven months until the assembly election.

The party has lost seats in the last two elections and now its losing seats in between elections.

stories.title: Chris Mason: Home secretary to face scrutiny over changes to rules for legal migrants
stories.summary: At the heart of the debate around legal migration are contested notions of fairness, our political editor writes.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 2 November 2026

At the heart of the debate around legal migration are contested notions of fairness.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has talked of her parents coming to the UK from rural Kashmir. Now, this daughter of immigrants is responsible for reshaping the very system that brought them here decades ago – and doing so in a way that both her party and the country regard as fair.

"Fair to those who seek a new and better life here, like my parents did. And fair to those already here, including British workers, and especially the young," is how Mahmood put it in her speech to the Labour Party conference in September.

The debate has come at a time of huge legal immigration in recent years and during a period in which Reform UK have been particularly prominent in the national political conversation.

Both of these things are factors in Labour wanting to be seen to be taking people's concerns about the scale of arrivals seriously.

But her political opponents smell what they see as weakness and retreat, with parts of her original plan now being revised, as the BBC's Iain Watson reported over the weekend .

It is worth examining this policy throughout the last year or so, as it is instructive in how we have arrived at today's announcement.

Mahmood to set out changes to settlement rules for legal migrants Published 7 hours ago

Fahnbulleh says she backs home secretary on migration after comments to journalists Published 22 October

Most people who come to the UK do so legally, after being granted a visa before they travel.

A visa gives someone permission to enter or stay in the UK for a specific purpose, such as work, study or joining family members.

There were 727,487 people who came to the UK via visas from July 2025 to June 2026, not including visitors or people transiting through the UK. This was down by 15% on the same period the previous year.

That does not mean all those people travelled to the UK, only that they were approved to do so.

The most common type of visa people came to the UK on was study, which made up 53% of all visa entries from July 2025 to June 2026.

People from China were the most common group to come to the UK on study visas, making up 23% of the total.

Together, people from China and India accounted for nearly half of all study visas. This has been the case for many years.

In November last year, Mahmood set out a plan called "a fairer pathway to settlement".

The idea was opinions on her instincts would be sought in a consultation. And boy, were there plenty of opinions offered.

Around 200,000 people contributed to the consultation, of which 140,000 responses came from visa holders themselves I'm told.

"It's been a colossal exercise and a genuine one," is how one Whitehall source put it to me, claiming: "We have taken the time to get this right."

Or is the real truth that they have buckled under political pressure from their own side – and a change of prime minister?

Mahmood said last year that she felt compelled to act because "between 2021 and 2024, we have seen net migration of an additional 2.6 million people. Around one in every 30 people in this country today arrived in these four years." It is what critics have labelled "the Boriswave", named for the changes made under former Prime Minister Boris Johnson.

And, Mahmood argued, it was important to act with urgency, as very soon significant numbers of those recent arrivals would start qualifying for indefinite leave to remain, or ILR.

"Migrants on lower wages who bring non-working dependants and children are likely to present significant fiscal costs to the UK.

"It is therefore right that we apply more stringent controls for this group before they qualify for settled status," she said, adding: "Under our current rules, they will usually qualify for benefits payments and council housing five years after arrival.

"As the majority of this group began arriving from 2022 onwards, this is currently set to begin in 2027. We consult here on a separate baseline qualifying period, of 15 years, for this group."

But plenty within the Labour Party and beyond were uncomfortable – and yes, they cited fairness, or the perceived lack of it, in mounting their criticisms.

As the now Housing Secretary Angela Rayner put it in March , before she returned to government, the ideas were "un-British" because they involved "moving the goalposts" - migrants who had arrived in good faith under one set of rules would have their future in the UK determined by the new ones.

Associated costs

Just a few weeks before Rayner's intervention, Mahmood had doubled down on her plans. Addressing the centre left IPPR think tank, she said "in just four years, this country experienced levels of migration it had previously seen across four decades.

"It was not just the scale, but also the nature of that change that was so destabilising."

There was more, and with a big number attached.

"We have never, in the history of this country, had so much low-skilled migration in so little time.

"We estimate, based on findings from the Migration Advisory Committee, that the lifetime cost to the taxpayer will be £10bn. That figure would be paid for by working people in this country."

She added: "It is an affront to the idea of fairness within our migration system."

Incidentally, the £10bn figure is contested by some – or at least placed in a wider context.

The aforementioned IPPR argue that the original plans were "never in reality going to create a £10bn long-term saving, given they were meant to delay care workers' eligibility for ILR rather than prevent them from settling altogether.

"Delaying ILR would save money on welfare, whereas the £10bn figure includes much broader long run costs once care workers enter retirement, claim the state pension, and make greater use of health and social care."

Nonetheless, Mahmood's message in March left senior Conservatives privately agreeing with her – and struck by her willingness to be unflinching in her approach to the subject.

But around 100 of her Labour colleagues were not happy – and making their views known publicly .

By the time I found myself in the dusty car park of a sports club near Wigan in May, waiting to talk to an ambitious by-election candidate by the name of Andy Burnham, it was clear changes were highly likely.

He told me it was important to "work hard to get the balance right" but that the "broad thrust" of what the home secretary was doing "is right".

"Broad thrust" will be the words that account for the gap between what Mahmood used to say and what she is saying today.

The Conservatives and others will seize upon the change. The Tories will argue it amounts to an "excruciating U-turn" as one senior figure described it to me, claiming it would be "deeply personally embarrassing" for the home secretary.

They also ponder how the government will choose to make the changes, as they believe if primary legislation isn't used to do it – such as via an amendment to the Immigration and Asylum Bill currently before parliament – the plans could be successfully challenged in court.

Mahmood will argue she has tried to finally arrive at a policy the widest range of people may see as fair.

We will see and hear the range of reaction she provokes in the coming hours and days.

stories.title: Government making up China policy as it goes along, say MPs
stories.summary: A report by the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee said decision-making had been characterised by "inconsistency".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Union flag was flown outside Tiananmen Gate, during Sir Keir Starmer's visit to Beijing in 2026

Published 2 November 2026

The government has failed to deliver on its promise to pursue a consistent approach towards China and is instead making up policy "as it goes along", MPs on the business committee have said.

The committee said in its report , external that decision-making had been characterised by "inconsistency" and was heightening national security risks.

It called on ministers to block the transfer of sensitive data to China, give businesses clear rules for doing trade with the super power and ban imports made using forced labour.

The business department said it disagreed with the report's conclusion adding: "Our approach to China is consistent - we will co-operate where we can and challenge where we must."

"We have placed our relationship on a more stable, balanced, long-term footing, and based it on a clear-eyed assessment of both the opportunities and the risks.

"Our trade strategy makes clear that we will capitalise on every opportunity to grow our economy while never compromising on our national security, and our increased discussions with China allows us to directly raise concerns where they arise."

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer had sought to pursue a closer relationship with China, arguing that the UK could not afford to ignore economic opportunities, while insisting that should not mean compromising on national security.

However, efforts to build ties were criticised by some MPs concerned about China's alleged spying activities in the UK.

An audit of the two countries' relationship was carried out last year , external but the government has not published the document in full, saying it contained classified information.

Sir Keir's successor Andy Burnham has yet to set out his position on relations with China.

China and the UK: After the golden era

High Court upholds decision to allow Chinese mega embassy Published 31 July

China hits out at British Steel nationalisation Published 17 July

In its report, the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee said successive governments had "failed to reassure" the public they had taken "adequate measures to defend UK national security and economic resilience".

The MPs said the unpredictability of government approaches and a lack of clear guidance had hindered businesses ability to trade with China.

It proposed setting up "red" and "green" zones to clearly defining where trade and investment would be encouraged and the areas which were "off limits".

The committee said that the government should insist on fair trade with China and advised preparing tariffs that could be imposed if the country continued to subsidise its industry or failed to offer "fully reciprocal" market access.

On protecting sensitive technology and data, the report said there should be a ban on connected technology devices being used in critical national infrastructure.

The committee said "low-cost" Chinese connected technology had become wide-spread in the UK and that in this area the government had "prioritised diplomatic politeness over the UK's national security".

Universities should also get "faster advice" on conducting research with Chinese bodies, it said.

Committee chair and Labour MP Liam Byrne said: "Britain's businesses cannot plan for the future when the government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along.

"Ministers promised clarity and consistency. Instead, we have opportunities missed, risks unmanaged and decisions left until the eleventh hour.

"Britain must shape its own relationship with China, or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing."

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Resolution Foundation study finds workers are less willing to go ‘above and beyond for employers than a decade ago’

Job satisfaction among UK workers has dropped to a record low, according to a study that shows a growing frustration with employers over pay and flexible working.

Analysis by the Resolution Foundation thinktank shows that a lack of flexible working, insecure jobs and a loss of independence have undermined how workers feel about their employment.

Based on the 2025 British Social Attitudes survey, the study found a sharp fall in satisfaction at work that translated into British workers being less willing to go “above and beyond for their employers than they were a decade ago”.

Job satisfaction fell from 81% in 2015 to 74%, the lowest figure recorded in the British Social Attitudes survey since 1989, when the question was first asked.

Fewer workers said they had an interesting job or one that offered the chance of advancement. The proportion of workers who said they would work harder than required to help their employer succeed fell from 69% in 2015 to 55% in 2025.

The Resolution Foundation said its analysis would give policymakers an insight into how they could reverse decades of slowing productivity growth, low levels of job mobility and high economic inactivity among some groups, most notably younger people .

Only 4% of workers said there was “little intrinsic value” from working – a figure that has remained flat over time. What has declined, the thinktank said, was the number of people feeling positive about the jobs they do.

The proportion saying they have an interesting job fell over the decade from 74% to 63%.

Hannah Slaughter, an economist at the foundation and co-author of the report, said there was a rise in the number of workers who said they suffered from low pay and this concern spanned all the pay scales.

She said decades of low pay-rises and the spiralling cost of living was affecting the outlook of all groups, though the demand for greater flexibility was equally pronounced.

after newsletter promotion

“Workers increasingly want jobs that provide flexibility, independence and financial security. But many feel those expectations are not being met,” said Slaughter.

“The result is rising frustration among workers, who report lower job satisfaction, declining willingness to go above and beyond, and a reduced appetite for full-time work. This ‘dissatisfaction drain’ is self-evidently bad for workers, but it also doesn’t bode well for productivity and labour supply, both of which are vital for lifting living standards in the years ahead.”

Separate polling by Ipsos dating back to the 1980s supported the foundation’s study, with workers reporting much lower satisfaction this year than when the same question was asked in 1976 and 1986. In 1976 it found 83% were very or fairly satisfied with their work compared with 69% in 2026.

John Curtice, the Strathclyde professor and pollster who is co-editor of the British Social Attitudes report, said the findings showed young people had not become more work-shy, “nor have workers in general become more reluctant to change jobs. But if workers are to be fully engaged in their work, it has seemingly become more important for employers to provide jobs that are both financial rewarding and have flexible work hours.”
